documents.markdown:
# Use this wiki

**Start with the task you need to complete and the material you can provide.** The catalog helps you choose a tool; profiles and guides help you prepare and interpret a check.

## Choose a tool for a known task

1. Open [Find a tool](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/) and use a task shortcut or search for a tool, language, or capability. Combine language and input filters: Python source analysis and Python dependency scanning answer different questions.
2. Read a candidate's setup, result, and limits. [Compare tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/) when you have two or three candidates, and check cost and edition details before choosing a workflow.
3. For several components or interfaces, use [Find tools for your system](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/analysis-suite/). Its candidates reflect reviewed prerequisites. Answer missing questions and check compatibility notes before treating a suggestion as ready to run.
4. Follow the profile's first-result procedure or a [worked Python workflow](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/python-checks/). Keep a [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/) and [review the findings](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/).

If you know the tool's name, search for it directly. Catalog search covers tool metadata; **Search all pages** also finds guide and profile text. Global sidebar category links start a fresh category view; category tabs above catalog results keep your current filters.

## Learn enough to choose

Start with [static versus dynamic analysis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/static-vs-dynamic/), then follow the route that matches your input:

- [Static analysis approaches](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/static-approaches/) separates source, binary, dependency, and configuration checks.
- [Ways to do DAST](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/dast-approaches/) explains testing a running application.
- [Verification and generated tests](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/verification-and-generated-tests/) distinguishes a proof, a counterexample, and a test result.

For a concrete choice, use the [Java](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/java-analysis/), [memory-error](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/memory-error-detection/), or [temporal monitoring](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/temporal-monitoring-and-falsification/) guide. [Research notes](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/) explain study findings and their limits.

## Read the evidence labels

A profile's verification date records documentation review. It is not a benchmark or proof that the example ran on your machine. Examples identify whether they are illustrative or executed; execution records name the environment and artifacts. Record your choice and unresolved prerequisites in an [adoption note](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/choosing-and-recording-tools/).

documents.markdown:
# Use ToolWiki with agents

Agents can read the same tool profiles, workflows, concepts, and research notes
that appear on this website. Start with static files if your agent can fetch
URLs. Use the local Model Context Protocol (MCP) server when you want named
tools for searching, reading, comparing, and selecting checks.

## Read the static export

Open the [knowledge manifest](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/manifest.json) and
[document index](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/index.json). The index lists stable document
IDs, website URLs, revisions, section IDs, and paths to Markdown and JSON records.
For example, read the [Python guide as Markdown](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/documents/guides/python-checks.md).

Resolve every file path relative to the manifest URL. For a consistent collection,
fetch the snapshot named in `manifest.snapshot.path`, then check its byte count
and SHA-256 against the manifest. The server performs these checks automatically.
A deployment can replace the available snapshot; if a fetch fails during an
update, fetch the manifest again and retry. Keep the validated snapshot for your
whole task. Individual index and document files can change between requests.

Revisions identify content, not dates. Tool review dates describe documentation
review. Recorded execution evidence names the tested environment and its limits;
`not-recorded` means that no structured execution record is supplied for that
document. It does not establish that an example fails or has never been run.

## Run the local MCP prototype

You need Git, Node.js 24, and pnpm 11.19.0. No service account or API key is needed
by this server. It reads knowledge and returns instructions; your agent's normal
tools execute commands only when your task calls for them.

1. Clone the repository and build its knowledge snapshot:

   ```powershell
   git clone https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki.git
   Set-Location ToolWiki
   pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
   pnpm build
   ```

2. Test the protocol from the repository root:

   ```powershell
   pnpm test:mcp
   ```

   Expect passing tests for discovery, tool calls, resources, errors, and clean
   shutdown. A build must exist before these tests run.

3. Register the server in your MCP client. For Codex, add this to your trusted
   project's `.codex/config.toml`, replacing the path with your clone's absolute
   path. Use forward slashes in Windows TOML strings:

   ```toml
   [mcp_servers.toolwiki]
   command = "node"
   args = ["--experimental-strip-types", "C:/path/to/ToolWiki/mcp/server.ts"]
   startup_timeout_sec = 30
   tool_timeout_sec = 30
   ```

   Start a fresh Codex session in that project. This configuration follows the
   [official Codex MCP instructions](https://learn.chatgpt.com/docs/extend/mcp?surface=cli).
   A client starts the server and communicates over standard input and output.
   Running `pnpm mcp` alone waits for that protocol; it does not open a web page.

4. Ask the agent to discover and follow a workflow:

   ```text
   Use ToolWiki MCP to find checks for Python lint and type errors. Read the
   prerequisites and evidence scope, then reproduce the faulty and corrected
   example in a scratch directory. Cite the document and snapshot revisions.
   ```

The default server reads the clone's `dist/knowledge/v1/manifest.json`, regardless
of the client's working directory. To use published knowledge instead, append
`"--manifest", "https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/knowledge/v1/manifest.json"`
to the `args` array. This still runs the MCP program locally; GitHub Pages hosts
the data. The server loads once at startup. Restart it after rebuilding or when
you want the latest published snapshot.

## Available operations

| Tool               | Use                                                                                            |
| ------------------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `search_knowledge` | Find document IDs with text, kind, and tool metadata filters.                                  |
| `get_document`     | Read a document or section, its sources, and evidence scope.                                   |
| `compare_tools`    | Compare two to four tool profiles using website metadata.                                      |
| `recommend_checks` | Evaluate a saved system-builder profile, including missing information and unmet requirements. |

The `toolwiki://snapshot` resource lists the pinned revision and document inventory.
See the [format and tool reference](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/agents-reference/) for inputs, limits,
pagination, and a complete recommendation example.

## Troubleshoot startup and results

- **Missing manifest:** run `pnpm build` in the clone, or check the explicit
  `--manifest` path. The server reports startup errors on standard error.
- **Integrity or fetch error:** rebuild local files, or retry a remote startup
  after deployment. The server rejects mixed or altered snapshots.
- **No tools appear:** check the Node executable, absolute script path, project
  trust, and your client's MCP startup log. Start a fresh client session.
- **No search results:** remove tool metadata filters when looking for a guide;
  those filters match tool profiles only. Try a shorter query.
- **Partial document:** continue `get_document` with `nextOffset` until it is
  `null`, retaining the same ID and section. Reassemble chunks before copying
  commands because a chunk can end inside a code block.

The initial supported connection is local stdio. Remote MCP hosting and hosted
authentication are deferred. A local server cannot make an untested platform
supported; follow each workflow's stated environment limits.

documents.title: Find a memory error on Windows
documents.description: Build a small C program with MSVC AddressSanitizer, diagnose an out-of-bounds write, and verify its correction.
documents.markdown:
# Find a memory error on Windows

Use MSVC AddressSanitizer to find an invalid write in a C program you can rebuild. You will compile a faulty example, read its diagnostic, and run a corrected version.

**Executed on native Windows Server 2022 x64**, with Visual Studio 2022 17.14.44 and MSVC 19.44.35229. The faulty write produced the expected diagnostic and the correction exited successfully; the [execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/a81760a9f74ed6d94eb33f80ab03f8bd6fc42362/audits/reader-workflows/implementation/memory/ci-42303178089/run.json) retains commands, versions, and checks. This route requires VS 2022 17.7 or later. Windows ARM64 and x64 emulation are outside its validated scope. The [Clang catalog entry](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/address-sanitizer/) covers a separate compiler integration.

## Prepare the compiler

You need native Windows x64, PowerShell, and Visual Studio 2022 with **Desktop development with C++**, the x64 MSVC tools, a Windows SDK, and **C++ AddressSanitizer**. Get the 2022 installer from Microsoft's [VS 2022 release page](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/releases/2022/release-history#release-dates-and-build-numbers), then follow its [C++ installation instructions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/build/vscpp-step-0-installation?view=msvc-170) and [AddressSanitizer component instructions](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/sanitizers/asan?view=msvc-170#install-addresssanitizer). These steps may require an administrator; this guide does not validate a fresh installation.

1. [Get the examples](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/get-examples/), then enter this directory from the extracted repository root:

   ```powershell
   Set-Location ./examples/windows-memory
   ```

2. Check your native host architecture before selecting the compiler. This must print `X64`:

   ```powershell
   [System.Runtime.InteropServices.RuntimeInformation]::OSArchitecture
   ```

   If it reports `Arm64`, stop and use a native Windows x64 machine. Selecting an x64 compiler does not change the host architecture.

3. Initialize the VS 2022 x64 developer shell in this PowerShell window:

   ```powershell
   $vswhere = "${env:ProgramFiles(x86)}/Microsoft Visual Studio/Installer/vswhere.exe"
   if (-not (Test-Path $vswhere)) { throw 'Install Visual Studio 2022 C++ tools first.' }
   $vs = & $vswhere -latest -products * -version '[17.7,18.0)' -requires Microsoft.VisualStudio.Component.VC.Tools.x86.x64 -property installationPath
   if (-not $vs) { throw 'VS 2022 17.7+ with x64 C++ tools was not found.' }
   & "$vs/Common7/Tools/Launch-VsDevShell.ps1" -Arch amd64 -HostArch amd64 -SkipAutomaticLocation
   ```

   This locates the installed edition and keeps your working directory. Microsoft documents these [developer-shell arguments](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/visualstudio/ide/reference/command-prompt-powershell?view=vs-2022#target-architecture-and-host-architecture).

4. Confirm the compiler, target, and runtime are ready:

   ```powershell
   cl
   $env:VSCMD_ARG_HOST_ARCH
   $env:VSCMD_ARG_TGT_ARCH
   $compiler = (Get-Command cl.exe -ErrorAction Stop).Source
   $runtime = Join-Path (Split-Path $compiler) 'clang_rt.asan_dynamic-x86_64.dll'
   if (-not (Test-Path $runtime)) { throw 'Add C++ AddressSanitizer in the VS 2022 Installer.' }
   ```

   The compiler banner must say `for x64`, and both architecture values must be `x64`. Bare `cl` may also print usage; no source is compiled in this preflight. The runtime DLL check verifies presence, while the corrected run below checks that it actually loads and runs.

## Diagnose the faulty write

`bad/bounds.c` allocates room for two integers, then writes index 2:

```c
#include <stdlib.h>
int main(void) {
    int *values = malloc(2 * sizeof(*values));
    if (!values) return 1;
    values[2] = 7;
    free(values);
    return 0;
}
```

1. Build it in the same PowerShell window:

   ```powershell
   New-Item -ItemType Directory -Path build -Force | Out-Null
   cl /nologo /Od /Zi /fsanitize=address ./bad/bounds.c /Fe:build/bad.exe /Fo:build/bad.obj /Fd:build/bad-compile.pdb /link /DEBUG /INCREMENTAL:NO
   if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Build failed; resolve the compiler or linker error before running.' }
   ```

   `/Od` disables optimization, `/Zi` and `/DEBUG` retain source attribution, and `/fsanitize=address` instruments memory accesses. Keep the generated `.pdb` files with the executables.

2. Run the faulty program and read its exit status:

   ```powershell
   ./build/bad.exe
   $LASTEXITCODE
   ```

   Expect a nonzero exit and a report containing the following markers. This is an expected outline, not captured output; addresses and stack formatting vary:

   ```text
   ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
   WRITE of size 4
   ... main ... bounds.c:5
   ```

   `heap-buffer-overflow` means the access crossed a heap allocation's boundary. The write stack identifies line 5; the allocation stack identifies the two-integer allocation. Only indices 0 and 1 fit. A process crash without this diagnostic is a failed setup or run, not a successful memory check.

## Verify the correction

The supplied `good/bounds.c` changes `values[2] = 7` to `values[1] = 7`. Build and run it with the same instrumentation:

```powershell
cl /nologo /Od /Zi /fsanitize=address ./good/bounds.c /Fe:build/good.exe /Fo:build/good.obj /Fd:build/good-compile.pdb /link /DEBUG /INCREMENTAL:NO
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Corrected build failed.' }
./build/good.exe
$LASTEXITCODE
```

Expect no AddressSanitizer error and exit status `0`. Success requires both the faulty program's diagnostic and the corrected program's clean run. If both crash, the experiment has not succeeded.

## Resolve setup failures

| Symptom                                                           | Next action                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Host architecture is `Arm64`                                      | Use native Windows x64 or the repository's `windows-2022` validation job. This route does not validate emulation.                                                                                                                                       |
| VS discovery fails, or `cl` is missing                            | Install or modify VS 2022 to add the C++ workload, then repeat developer-shell initialization.                                                                                                                                                          |
| Compiler or target is not x64                                     | Open a fresh PowerShell window and repeat initialization with both `-Arch amd64` and `-HostArch amd64`.                                                                                                                                                 |
| ASan library/DLL is missing, including `LNK1356`                  | Add C++ AddressSanitizer through the VS 2022 Installer. Run from the initialized developer shell so its runtime directory is on PATH. See [Microsoft's runtime reference](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/sanitizers/asan-runtime?view=msvc-170). |
| Report has no source line                                         | Rebuild with `/Zi` and `/DEBUG` and retain `.pdb` files. [Symbolization is on by default](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/cpp/sanitizers/asan-flags?view=msvc-170); check that existing `ASAN_OPTIONS` settings do not disable it.                    |
| Both programs crash, or the bad program lacks the expected report | Treat this as a failed environment/run. Save both outputs, exit statuses, compiler version, and host/target architecture before investigating.                                                                                                          |

When adapting this to your program, keep the build flags and triggering input with each report. A clean run only covers the code that executed; it does not establish that every input is safe. [Choose other memory-error checks](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/memory-error-detection/) when you need uninitialized-value checks, executable-only analysis, or another platform.

documents.markdown:
# Research overview

I summarize research with my collaborators and its implications for developers using static analysis to assess software security and quality.

## Topics

- **[Comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/).** An empirical study of detection patterns across twelve Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP) implementations, with attention to language-specific analysis capabilities.
- **[SAST adoption](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/sast-adoption/).** A literature review of usability problems that affect adoption and continued use, including false positives, poor output, setup effort, and workflow disruption.
- **[SAST in CI/CD](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/sast-workflow/).** A process for transferring SAST findings into existing issue-tracking software, demonstrated with SonarQube and GitLab.
- **[Software quality models](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/software-quality/).** A proposed application of hierarchical software quality assurance (HSQA) to electric vehicle charging software, connecting analysis results to quality and security characteristics.
- **[Malware sophistication](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/binary-analysis/).** A proposed approach to malware quality assessment using characteristics that can be investigated through static binary analysis.

## Related tools

The **Related research** section on a tool page explains its role in the corresponding work. Some tools were used in an empirical study or implementation; others were discussed as possible inputs to a quality model.

Where a paper does not identify a product edition, the connection is labeled **Related product family**. Consult the tool profile for capabilities, configuration requirements, and licensing within its stated edition and version scope. Study results describe the configurations used in the research.

## Papers

I distinguish recommendations from our reported results.

My [master's thesis, On Improving the Adoption, Usability, and Retention of Static Application Security Testing (SAST) Tools](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/thesis/Wadhams.pdf) brings together the adoption review and CI/CD work. Its chapters and the corresponding conference papers describe the same research.

My [Google Scholar profile](https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=fcOP0tgAAAAJ\&hl=en) lists these papers and my NVMeoF internship project.

documents.description: Software quality characteristics and measurement limitations in static malware analysis.
documents.markdown:
# Malware sophistication

In [Characterizing and Codifying Malware Sophistication](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/iETC_Porcella_2026.pdf), we examined how software quality concepts can inform assessments of malware when only compiled artifacts are available.

## Approach

We define sophistication in terms of the specialized knowledge and effort involved in development. We hypothesize that malware quality provides a partial measure of sophistication. We do not yet know how to measure that knowledge and effort directly.

We adapt selected ISO/IEC 25010 characteristics: reliability, security, maintainability, and flexibility. We consider which properties could be investigated through static binary analysis.

## Limitations

Source-dependent metrics may be unavailable, and obfuscation can distort recovered structure. Apparent code complexity therefore requires interpretation. We discuss cwe-checker as a tool that can identify selected reliability-related weaknesses in binaries.

Applying the proposed approach to malware samples and validating the assessments remain future work.

## Interpreting findings

When interpreting a binary-analysis report, I would retain the following information:

| Analysis consideration | Information to retain                                                                         |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Artifact               | Binary format, target architecture, and the component being examined.                         |
| Code recovery          | Functions and APIs recovered or modeled, along with failures and unsupported features.        |
| Measured property      | The reported weakness or structural feature and the method used to identify it.               |
| Quality interpretation | The characteristic the observation may inform and the assumptions supporting that connection. |
| Uncertainty            | Effects of packing, obfuscation, missing code, and incomplete models.                         |

Review analysis coverage before interpreting the number of findings. A tool that could not recover relevant code provides limited evidence about that code's quality.

These considerations support interpretation of tool output. I do not present them as a validated sophistication metric.

## Related tools

[cwe-checker](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cwe-checker/) examines recovered code for weakness patterns. We discuss it in connection with possible reliability measurements. We did not conduct a comparative evaluation of binary analyzers.

We also discuss [Ghidra](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ghidra/), [capa](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/capa/), and YARA in the context of binary analysis and obfuscation. Ghidra provides recovered code structure, while capa matches features to capability rules. I include [YARA-X](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/yara-x/) as a related successor to YARA; our paper does not evaluate YARA-X. These outputs support different questions and should not be combined into a sophistication score without validation.

[CVE Binary Tool](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cve-bin-tool/) provides a related workflow based on component identification and advisory matching. I link it here to clarify the distinction between binary-analysis inputs and analysis purpose. We did not evaluate it in the malware paper.

Use the [Binaries filter](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/static/?input=Binaries) and each tool's scope to identify an appropriate workflow.

## Paper

Angelo Porcella, Zachary Wadhams, Clemente Izurieta, Jonathan Crussell, and Ann Marie Reinhold. **Characterizing and Codifying Malware Sophistication.** IEEE I-ETC, 2026. [Read the author copy](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/iETC_Porcella_2026.pdf), especially Sections III-V.

Related notes: [static analysis approaches](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/static-approaches/) and [software quality models](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/software-quality/).

documents.description: Detection patterns and language-specific analysis capabilities in twelve OCPP implementations.
documents.markdown:
# Comparing SAST tools

**When choosing tools:** compare what they actually check before comparing finding counts. Our study describes detection patterns, not an accuracy ranking.

In our [OCPP study](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf), we examined how static application security testing (SAST) findings vary across programming languages and their analysis tools. We used implementations of the Open Charge Point Protocol (OCPP) as our software corpus.

## Methods

We selected twelve open-source OCPP 1.6 implementations, with one project per language. We ran SonarQube, Semgrep, and language-specific analyzers using default configurations and examined the number and types of reported issues.

## Findings

Across the implementations we analyzed, the tools reported 4,660 findings, approximately 89% of which were classified as code quality or maintainability issues. Totals ranged from two for Rust to 1,689 for Java.

Detection scope contributed to these differences. Broader quality checks and narrower bug-pattern checks produced different reports. Tool execution also affected interpretation: Semgrep failed on the C project, while some other combinations completed without findings.

## Limitations

We analyzed one implementation per language and did not validate false positives or false negatives. Project size, configuration, and differences in analysis scope limit direct comparison. The results describe detection patterns; they do not establish relative security or isolate tool maturity as the cause of variation.

## Tool selection

For a new evaluation, I recommend considering:

- **Language-specific capabilities.** Check the relevant rules, supported frameworks, and required inputs. A shared language label does not establish equivalent analysis coverage.
- **Complementary analysis.** Consider whether a specialized analyzer examines issue categories that a broader tool covers less extensively.
- **Comparable conditions.** Record the project revision, tool version and edition, enabled rules, exclusions, and analysis status.
- **Finding validation.** Review results before comparing their practical value. Examine duplicate reports and review effort when combining tools.

I use the [catalog comparison](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/) to present documented capabilities. Evaluating those capabilities on representative code requires a separate analysis.

## Related tools

We used [SonarQube](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/sonarqube/), Semgrep, [Cppcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cppcheck/), [gosec](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/gosec/), [SpotBugs](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/spotbugs/), [detekt](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/detekt/), [Psalm](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/psalm/), [Bandit](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/bandit/), [Brakeman](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/brakeman/), [cargo-audit](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cargo-audit/), and [WartRemover](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/wartremover/). Our tool table also lists NodeJsScan for JavaScript and Roslyn for C#.

I link [the .NET SDK analyzers](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/dotnet-analyzers/) as related Roslyn-based tooling. The paper does not identify the exact Roslyn package or rule set, so I do not assign our C# results to the current SDK defaults.

Cargo-audit matches dependency versions to advisories; it does not inspect Rust source logic for new defects. I retain that scope distinction when comparing its findings with those of source analyzers. Likewise, a tool name does not establish use of every optional mode: Psalm's separate taint analysis and detekt's type-resolution tasks need explicit configuration.

I list [Semgrep CE](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/semgrep-ce/) and [Semgrep Code](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/semgrep-code/) separately, as I do [SonarQube Community Build](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/sonarqube-community/) and Server. Our paper does not provide enough edition detail to assign the findings to these current offerings.

## Paper

Zachary Wadhams, Emma Sheppard, Dalton Arford, Clemente Izurieta, and Ann Marie Reinhold. **How Well Do SAST Tools Work Across Languages? An Empirical Study Using OCPP Implementations.** IEEE CSR, 2026. [Read the author copy](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf), especially Sections III-V.

Related notes: [static analysis approaches](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/static-approaches/) and [SAST adoption](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/sast-adoption/).

documents.markdown:
# SAST adoption

**When evaluating a tool:** try the complete cycle of setup, reviewing findings, and fixing an issue. The ongoing effort matters as much as the first run.

In [Barriers to Using SAST Tools](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01669), we examined the problems developers encounter when adopting and using static application security testing. We focused on usability and the technical and human factors that affect continued use.

## Methods

We reviewed 89 papers selected from ACM and IEEE conference literature covering 2019-2023. We identified recurring problems and recorded how frequently each was mentioned.

## Findings

We identified barriers including false positives, poor output, time-consuming setup, manual effort to fix issues, and workflow disruption. More than two-thirds of the reviewed papers mentioned false positives. This measures the prevalence of a reported concern in the literature, not tool accuracy.

We argue that both development teams and tool creators have a role in improving adoption. Developers invest effort in configuration and interpretation; tool creators can improve output, setup, remediation guidance, and integration.

## Limitations

We examined the range and frequency of reported problems. We did not measure their severity in every development environment. Our databases, search terms, selection criteria, and time window limit the literature represented.

## Evaluating usability

I would ask:

| Usability concern   | Question for an initial evaluation                                                        |
| ------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| False positives     | How much investigation is required, and how are reviewed decisions retained?              |
| Output quality      | Does the report explain the issue, affected code, and information needed for remediation? |
| Setup               | What configuration and maintenance does the tool require?                                 |
| Manual effort       | What guidance is available for understanding and resolving findings?                      |
| Workflow disruption | When does analysis run, where are results presented, and who addresses them?              |

Evaluate these aspects over several analysis runs. Initial setup alone does not account for the ongoing work of maintaining rules and reviewing findings.

For a current procedure, use [Review analysis findings](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/) to check completion, investigate a report, record a disposition, and verify a repair. [Repeatable CI checks](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/ci-checks/) covers result handling and gates. These guides are practical follow-up advice, separate from the literature review's findings.

I include **What it examines**, **What you need**, and **Checks and limits** in the tool profiles to help prepare an evaluation. Experience in the intended development environment is still needed to assess usability.

## Paper

Zachary Wadhams, Clemente Izurieta, and Ann Marie Reinhold. **Barriers to Using Static Application Security Testing (SAST) Tools: A Literature Review.** ASEW, 2024, pp. 161-166. [Read the paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.01669), especially Sections 3-5. The conference paper is from 2024; its arXiv posting is from 2026.

My [master's thesis](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/thesis/Wadhams.pdf) connects the review to the [CI/CD integration use case](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/sast-workflow/). See also [comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/).

documents.markdown:
# SAST in CI/CD

**When planning an integration:** make findings understandable where developers already work, and decide how reviews and duplicate reports will be handled.

In our [CI/CD paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00676), we presented a process for connecting SAST output with existing issue-tracking software. We wanted to make findings accessible within the development environment and support remediation.

## Process

A controller script collects SAST results, formats the relevant information, and sends it to the issue tracker. We worked with an organization that used Python to connect SonarQube with GitLab. Network restrictions had limited direct SonarQube access to two senior developers in a team of more than twenty.

Generated issues included code context, explanations, and weakness or vulnerability references. The process prevented duplicate issue creation. Nightly analysis was followed by a merge-request quality gate.

## Findings

Developers responded positively to the presentation and accessibility of findings. Reported challenges included a learning curve, effort to identify false positives, and conflicting views about quality-gate restrictions.

## Limitations

Our use case involved one organization and one SAST tool. The feedback does not establish effectiveness across other tools or development environments. Current integration details also depend on the selected product version and APIs.

## Integration

When adapting the process to another environment, I would consider:

1. **Analysis completion.** Check that analysis completed before collecting results, and retain execution errors for investigation.
2. **Issue selection and formatting.** Define the relevant finding categories and include code location, rule information, and context needed for remediation.
3. **Duplicate prevention.** Maintain the association between findings and tracker issues across repeated analysis runs.
4. **Review and resolution.** Distinguish transferring a finding from determining its validity or resolving it.
5. **Quality gates.** Establish conditions appropriate to the development environment and review their effect on developer workflow.

I provide these as implementation considerations; this wiki does not supply a tested connector. A passing quality gate means its configured conditions were met.

[Repeatable CI checks](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/ci-checks/) applies these considerations to the wiki's Ruff and mypy recipe, including run states, retained artifacts, and an explicit gate. [Review analysis findings](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/) covers investigation and disposition. These procedures do not reproduce the study's SonarQube/GitLab integration.

## Related tools

We used SonarQube. I list [Server](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/sonarqube/) and [Community Build](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/sonarqube-community/), but our study does not compare those current editions.

For other tools, examine report formats, finding identifiers, result states, and API access before adapting the process.

## Paper

Zachary Wadhams, Ann Marie Reinhold, and Clemente Izurieta. **Automating Static Code Analysis Through CI/CD Pipeline Integration.** SANER-C, 2024, pp. 119-125. [Read the paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00676), especially Sections IV-VII. The arXiv posting is from 2026.

Related notes: [SAST adoption](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/sast-adoption/) and [SAST vs. DAST](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/sast-vs-dast/).

documents.description: Applying HSQA to evaluate quality and security characteristics in electric vehicle charging software.
documents.markdown:
# Software quality models

In [Wicked Problem, Parsimonious Solution](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/Sheppard_CSR_2025.pdf), we proposed applying hierarchical software quality assurance (HSQA) to electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) software. Our approach connects analysis results with broader characteristics used to assess software quality and security.

## Approach

HSQA aggregates tool outputs through levels of a quality model. We discuss PIQUE, the Platform for Investigative software Quality Understanding and Evaluation, as an implementation approach.

We drew the proposed EVSE characteristics from software quality standards, charging-infrastructure cybersecurity practices, and standards from related infrastructure domains. We proposed combining assessments of software components that operate together.

## Coverage

An HSQA model depends on the characteristics its analysis tools can measure. We identified limited EVSE-specific tooling as a threat to validity and discussed SonarQube and CVE Binary Tool as inputs to the work described in the paper.

Our paper advocates an application of HSQA. We do not validate a universal security score or establish that static analysis measures every relevant characteristic.

## Model design

When reviewing a proposed model, I would ask:

- **Characteristics and sub-characteristics.** Which aspects of quality and security are relevant to the software and its operating context?
- **Measures.** Which tool outputs represent each characteristic, and what assumptions support those mappings?
- **Coverage.** Which components or characteristics cannot be assessed with the available tools?
- **Aggregation.** How are outputs normalized and combined, and how are overlapping findings handled?
- **Interpretation.** What conclusions are supported by the measurements and the model's assumptions?

Keep the original reports and analysis configuration available when interpreting an aggregate result. Missing measurements should remain distinguishable from favorable observations. I offer these as model-review considerations; this wiki does not implement a scoring formula.

## Related tools

[SonarQube](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/sonarqube/) provides code-analysis findings. [CVE Binary Tool](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cve-bin-tool/) identifies components and associates them with known vulnerability information. These outputs represent different types of evidence; see [static analysis approaches](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/static-approaches/).

We discuss PIQUE in the paper. I have not yet added a separately verified catalog entry for it.

## Paper

Emma Sheppard, Zachary Wadhams, Dalton Arford, Clemente Izurieta, and Ann Marie Reinhold. **Wicked Problem, Parsimonious Solution: Securing Electric Vehicle Charging Station Software.** IEEE CSR, 2025, pp. 679-686. [Read the author copy](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/Sheppard_CSR_2025.pdf), especially Sections III-V.

Related notes: [comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/) and [malware sophistication](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/binary-analysis/).

documents.markdown: # actionlint ## Where it fits actionlint can catch workflow problems before a CI run. It understands workflow keys and expression types, giving it a more specific role than a general YAML parser. ## First try **Illustrative example; not executed here.** Use the [actionlint 1.7.7 release](https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint/releases/tag/v1.7.7) archive matching your host OS and CPU, and record `actionlint -version`. Save this local file as `workflow.yml`; there is no need to upload it to GitHub: ```yaml name: Example on: push jobs: check: runs-on: ubuntu-latest steps: - run: echo ready unexpected-key: true ``` Check the workflow structure with the optional script linters disabled: ```sh actionlint -shellcheck= -pyflakes= workflow.yml ``` Expect an unexpected-key diagnostic for the step. Remove `unexpected-key: true` and rerun; that diagnostic should disappear. This exercises actionlint's own workflow checks without installing ShellCheck or Pyflakes. The [check reference](https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint/blob/main/docs/checks.md#check-unexpected-keys) and [usage guide](https://github.com/rhysd/actionlint/blob/main/docs/usage.md) describe the diagnostic and integration flags. For a real repository, check its `.github/workflows` files and configure custom runner labels when needed. Enable external script linters deliberately; [ShellCheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/shellcheck/) findings still depend on the selected shell context. ## Read the diagnostic context Review the expression, input, or workflow field named by the report. Keep a real CI run as part of validation: credentials, network access, service behavior, and job runtime are outside a static workflow check.

documents.title: AddressSanitizer (Clang)
documents.description: Detect selected memory errors while executing a program built with AddressSanitizer instrumentation.
documents.markdown: # AddressSanitizer (Clang) ## Where it fits AddressSanitizer adds a memory-error detector to executions generated by tests or fuzzers. It pairs naturally with [AFL++](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/afl-plus-plus/) or [libFuzzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/libfuzzer/). For a native Windows x64 route using Visual Studio 2022, follow [Find a memory error on Windows with MSVC](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/windows-memory-check/). That separate guide states its validation status and supplies setup, a faulty run, and a correction. This catalog entry and its metadata remain specific to Clang/LLVM. ## First try **Illustrative example, not run here.** With Clang and its sanitizer runtime installed on a supported host, save `bounds.c`: ```c #include int main(void) { int *values = malloc(2 * sizeof(*values)); if (!values) return 1; values[2] = 7; free(values); return 0; } ``` Build and run this small test in a Unix-style shell on a supported host: ```sh clang -O0 -g -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer bounds.c -o bounds ./bounds ``` For Windows PowerShell, use a compiler environment with `clang`, its C linker/libraries, and the matching AddressSanitizer runtime available. This uses the `clang` driver, not `clang-cl`; these commands are also illustrative and have not been run here: ```powershell clang -O0 -g -fsanitize=address -fno-omit-frame-pointer bounds.c -o bounds.exe .\bounds.exe ``` Before choosing this route, confirm the compiler target and runtime match your executable's architecture. A Windows label alone does not establish that your toolchain or dependencies are compatible. Representative report outline, not captured output; addresses and most stack frames are omitted: ```text ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 4 #0 main ... bounds.c:5 ... allocated ... #0 ... malloc ... #1 main ... bounds.c:3 ``` The error names the kind of invalid access. The first stack points to the write, and the allocation stack points to the two-element allocation. Index 2 is outside that allocation; valid indices are 0 and 1. Correct the index and repeat. The report format and symbol locations depend on the platform and available debug information. For toolchain installation and platform-specific setup, use the [Clang AddressSanitizer guide](https://clang.llvm.org/docs/AddressSanitizer.html). ## Interpret coverage A successful execution only covers the behavior that ran. Keep the build flags, workload, and suppression settings with the report. See [memory-error detection](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/memory-error-detection/) to compare an instrumented build with static checking and Memcheck's executable instrumentation. If you only have an existing executable, check [Memcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/valgrind-memcheck/) or [Dr. Memory](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/dr-memory/) for a compatible host and binary. They use different runtime checking workflows; check the platform limits before choosing one.

documents.description: Mutate inputs using execution feedback to find crashes, hangs, and failures exposed by a fuzzing target.
documents.markdown:
# AFL++

## What it does

AFL++ evolves a collection of input samples using feedback from repeated target executions. Inputs that expose new behavior help guide later mutations. It saves interesting failures so you can reproduce and investigate them.

The target may read input from a file or standard input, or use a custom harness for a library. A small deterministic target generally makes failures easier to reproduce.

## Source available versus binary only

With source, compile the target with compatible instrumentation. Without source, a supported mode can obtain feedback through mechanisms such as emulation or dynamic instrumentation. Those modes have distinct platform and architecture restrictions.

Both workflows execute a binary. This is dynamic testing, even though a source build or binary preparation step happens first.

## What counts as a failure?

Crashes and timeouts are useful starting points. A sanitizer can make otherwise silent memory errors visible; an assertion can expose a violated invariant. Without an appropriate failure detector, an incorrect output may look like an ordinary successful execution.

Deduplicate and replay failures before estimating their significance. More coverage or more saved crashes does not directly measure the number of distinct vulnerabilities.

See [verification and generated tests](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/verification-and-generated-tests/) for the comparison with property-based testing and temporal falsification.

# angr

## When to use it

Choose angr when the question is about behavior inside a compiled artifact and you can write the analysis needed to answer it. For a predefined set of binary weakness checks, compare [cwe-checker](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cwe-checker/).

## Worked example: find an input for a branch

**Illustrative example, not run here.** On a compatible native build host, save `branch_check.c`:

```c
#include <stdio.h>
int main(void) {
    puts(getchar() == 'K' ? "accepted" : "rejected");
    return 0;
}
```

Compile it with `cc -O0 branch_check.c -o branch_check`. In a Python environment with angr installed, run:

```python
import angr
import claripy

project = angr.Project("./branch_check", auto_load_libs=False)
symbol = claripy.BVS("input_byte", 8)
stream = angr.SimFileStream(name="stdin", content=symbol, has_end=True)
state = project.factory.full_init_state(args=["./branch_check"], stdin=stream)
paths = project.factory.simulation_manager(state)
paths.explore(find=lambda candidate: b"accepted" in candidate.posix.dumps(1))

if paths.found:
    print(paths.found[0].posix.dumps(0))
else:
    print("No matching state found in this exploration")
```

The intended witness is the byte `K`. This is a reachability exercise; the branch is not itself a security defect.

## Limits

Models of library calls, startup state, memory, and system behavior affect the result. Many branches can make exploration expensive. Finding no state does not establish impossibility unless the exploration and model justify that conclusion.

Reproduce a witness against the original program before drawing conclusions about concrete behavior.

See [static method results](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/advanced-static-methods/) to distinguish symbolic path constraints from concrete execution.

# Bandit

## What it does

Bandit parses Python files and runs security checks against their abstract syntax trees. Its plugins look for patterns associated with unsafe behavior and produce findings for review.

## When it is useful

Use it as a focused security check in a Python development workflow.

## What to keep in mind

A flagged pattern needs context: an API call may be intentional, or its input may already be constrained. Bandit is not a proof that a project is secure, and its checks do not replace runtime testing or a review of application logic.

## Getting started

The official documentation links installation, configuration, plugin, and CI/CD guides. Begin with the default checks on a small Python project, then review findings before adding exclusions.

## Related research

**Used in a study:** The [OCPP paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf) used Bandit for its Python implementation. Its results illustrate how a focused analyzer can produce a different report from a multi-language platform. They do not establish that every reported pattern is a confirmed vulnerability.

documents.markdown:
# Binwalk

## What it does

Binwalk helps identify what a firmware image or other binary container may contain. A result gives an offset and a candidate format, which can guide extraction and inspection of an embedded filesystem, archive, or executable.

## Example

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** In a supported Binwalk 3 environment, scan a firmware image you already have:

```sh
binwalk firmware.bin
```

Review the reported offsets and formats. Enable extraction separately if needed, using the release's documented options and extractor dependencies. The command above is the initial identification step.

## Limits

A recognizable header is evidence of a candidate format, not a guarantee that extraction will succeed. Compression and encryption can both affect entropy, so an entropy result needs context.

Binwalk does not by itself determine whether an embedded component has a known CVE. After locating an artifact, use [CVE Binary Tool](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cve-bin-tool/) for supported component/advisory matching or [Ghidra](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ghidra/) to inspect recovered code. Keep the original image and offsets so findings can be traced back to their source.

documents.markdown:
# boofuzz

## What it does

boofuzz separates the protocol description from the target connection and failure monitoring. A request graph can establish a session before mutating a later message. Supported connections include TCP, UDP, and serial interfaces.

## First try

Use the [supplied PING target and harness](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/protocol-ping) for a complete local response check. It includes a loopback server, faulty and corrected modes, two selected mutations, response validation, readiness/reset handling, and stop instructions.

**Executed on 2026-11-06:** boofuzz 0.4.2 on Windows/Python 3.12.16. The faulty target omitted its reply to a valid `PING TRIGGER` request. The response callback reported that violation; the corrected target passed both selected cases. This was a finite protocol demonstration, not a process-crash test or a broad fuzzing campaign.

Each run retains requests, replies, configuration hashes, console output, and a boofuzz database. The [execution observations](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/audits/remaining-work/executions/boofuzz) preserve the results separately from expected behavior. Adapt the message model, monitor, and reset procedure to the real target before expanding the mutation set.

## Limits

A lost connection may be expected rejection or a real failure; inspect the service and reproduce the input. Protocol state, checksums, authentication, and target recovery can require custom harness work.

Compare [Schemathesis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/schemathesis/) or [RESTler](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/restler/) when an HTTP API definition can drive test generation. Compare [AFL++](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/afl-plus-plus/) when an instrumentable binary and execution-feedback workflow fit better.

documents.markdown:
# Brakeman

## When to use it

Choose Brakeman when you have a Rails codebase and want checks that understand Rails conventions. General Ruby syntax support in another analyzer does not establish equivalent knowledge of Rails data flow.

## Worked example: review a Rails project

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** Install the current compatible gem, then run from the root of a Rails project you can review:

```sh
gem install brakeman
brakeman -o brakeman-report.html
```

Open the report and inspect the warning's location, confidence, and evidence. For a concrete exercise, review a controller that incorporates request data into a SQL string. Compare it with the corresponding parameterized query and re-run the scanner. Exact warnings depend on Rails version and the surrounding code.

## Free use and commercial use

The license explicitly treats scanning the licensee's own software as a permitted free use. Its defined commercial uses include offering a scanning service and distributing the scanner in a commercial product. Read the linked terms for your workflow.

Source availability does not make this an unrestricted open-source license. The catalog therefore uses Source available and Free with limits.

## What a result means

A source warning is a review lead. It does not show that authentication, routing, or deployed configuration makes the path reachable. Conversely, an unrecognized pattern can escape a check.

Combine source review with [ZAP](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/zap/) or another suitable runtime test when you need evidence about a running Rails application.

## Related research

**Used in a study:** The [OCPP paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf) lists Brakeman as its Ruby analyzer. That historical selection does not broaden Brakeman's documented Rails scope to arbitrary Ruby applications.

Read [comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/) for the study's limitations. For a new evaluation, verify that the application's framework matches the tool before interpreting its report.

# Breach

## What it does

Breach can check recorded signals against Signal Temporal Logic (STL) requirements or repeatedly simulate a model to search for a violation. It provides Simulink integration, parameter exploration, input signal generation, and an interface for other simulators.

## When it is useful

Use it when a requirement concerns behavior over time: for example, whether a controller keeps a signal below a limit throughout a run.

## What you provide

- A simulator interface or recorded traces with named signals.
- An STL requirement and a simulation horizon.
- For falsification, allowed input or parameter ranges and a search budget.

## What to keep in mind

A monitor checks supplied traces; a falsification search generates candidates to find a violating trace. An unsuccessful search does not prove the requirement holds for all inputs. See [model and temporal falsification](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/model-falsification/).

## Getting started

Follow the official README's setup and built-in demos, then work through its falsification example. Check the licenses of bundled components as well as the core license if redistributing the toolbox.

documents.markdown:
# capa

## Inputs

For static analysis, capa extracts features from supported artifacts such as PE, ELF, .NET modules, or shellcode. For dynamic analysis, it reads recorded behavior from a supported sandbox report. These workflows do not necessarily expose the same evidence.

The Dynamic tag describes analysis of previously observed execution. Passing a binary to the ordinary static workflow does not run it in a sandbox.

## Example

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** With the standalone release and its bundled resources, inspect a known test executable:

```sh
capa -vv sample.exe
```

Review each matched rule and its evidence locations. Follow interesting locations in [Ghidra](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ghidra/) before drawing conclusions about the surrounding behavior.

## Limits

Packing can expose mostly the unpacker rather than the payload. An installer can expose its installation framework rather than the installed program. Missing features, unsupported code, and incomplete sandbox coverage all limit matching.

A capability such as file access can be ordinary application behavior. Record the rule set and analysis mode alongside the result.

## Related research

We discuss capa in our [malware sophistication paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/iETC_Porcella_2026.pdf) as part of the binary-analysis context. We did not evaluate its accuracy or validate a capability count as a sophistication measure. See [Malware sophistication](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/binary-analysis/) for those limits.

# cargo-audit

## Inputs

The project workflow reads `Cargo.lock` to identify resolved dependencies and consults the RustSec advisory database. It does not execute the application or require a source-analysis build.

The binary workflow can use dependency information embedded by `cargo auditable`. Without that metadata, recovery from panic strings is partial and can miss Rust crates and embedded C components. The Binaries tag therefore does not promise a complete inventory of every Rust executable.

## Example

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** With Cargo installed:

```sh
cargo install cargo-audit --locked
```

From a project containing `Cargo.lock`, run:

```sh
cargo audit
```

For a supported release's binary workflow:

```sh
cargo audit bin path/to/program
```

Review each identified version and advisory. Preserve the lockfile or binary revision and advisory-data date with the report.

## Limits

An inventory/advisory match is not a source defect diagnosis. For Rust source checks, compare [Clippy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/clippy/) or [Kani](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/kani/). For multiple dependency ecosystems, compare [OSV-Scanner](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/osv-scanner/).

## Related research

We used Cargo-audit for Rust in our [OCPP study](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf). Its dependency-advisory results differ in scope from source-analyzer results; see [Comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/).

documents.title: CBMC
documents.description: Check C and C++ assertions and memory safety by translating bounded program executions into solver queries.
documents.markdown: # CBMC ## What it does CBMC converts a representation of possible C/C++ executions into constraints for a solver. It checks selected safety properties and assertions and can return a counterexample showing inputs and steps that violate a property. This can reveal defects beyond the concrete inputs in an ordinary test suite. Useful targets include small routines with strict memory-safety requirements or explicit input/output contracts. ## Bounds and proof claims Loops are unwound to explore iterations. If a chosen bound cuts off possible behavior, checking within that bound does not establish correctness beyond it. Unwinding assertions help determine whether further iterations remain possible. The harness also matters. Assumptions restrict inputs, and models of external functions determine which effects the verifier considers. An overly restrictive assumption can exclude the very behavior you intended to check. ## First try **Illustrative example; not executed here.** Install a CBMC 6.x build for your host using the [official setup guide](https://model-checking.github.io/cbmc-training/installation.html). Save this as `bounded.c`: ```c #include int nondet_int(void); int clamp(int value) { return value; } void harness(void) { int value = nondet_int(); __CPROVER_assume(value >= 0 && value <= 10); assert(clamp(value) <= 9); } ``` Use `harness` as the entry point and request a counterexample: ```sh cbmc bounded.c --function harness --trace ``` CBMC treats the undefined `nondet_int` return as nondeterministic. The assumption restricts it to 0 through 10. Expect the assertion to fail with `value = 10`. Change the function to `return value > 9 ? 9 : value;` and rerun. That assertion should pass under the stated assumption. This fixture has no loops, recursion, or external side effects, so it needs no loop bound. When adapting it to looping code, supply suitable unwinding bounds and inspect unwinding assertions as well as the property. Do not suppress an incomplete unwind and call the result an unbounded proof. Keep the harness, assumptions, checked properties, and bounds with the [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). The [harness guide](https://model-checking.github.io/cbmc-training/cbmc/overview/proof-harnesses.html) and [property-checking guide](https://model-checking.github.io/cbmc-training/cbmc/overview/checking-properties.html) explain how these choices define the verification task. See [verification and generated tests](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/verification-and-generated-tests/) for the difference between bounded checking, fuzzing, and falsification.

# Clang Static Analyzer

## What it does

Clang Static Analyzer performs path-sensitive analysis to find bugs in C-family programs. It reasons about possible execution paths without running the target program on concrete test inputs.

## When it is useful

Consider it when working on native code and investigating defects such as invalid pointer use. It is part of Clang and can fit into a build-oriented workflow.

## What to keep in mind

The analyzer needs an accurate view of the code and build configuration. Its modeled paths do not cover all possible program behavior. Review the available checkers and their maturity before treating their output as equally reliable.

## Getting started

Follow the analyzer's documentation for a build-integrated run. Keep the compiler configuration and enabled checker set with your results so later runs are comparable.

See [clang-tidy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/clang-tidy/) for a configurable linting and modernization workflow that can also select Clang Static Analyzer checks. [Compare the two tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Fclang-static-analyzer%2Ctools%2Fclang-tidy) before choosing the checks to run.

# clang-tidy

## Where it fits

Use clang-tidy for repeatable source checks during development or code review. Select the check families your project needs, and record the configuration in `.clang-tidy`.

It can invoke checks from [Clang Static Analyzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/clang-static-analyzer/), alongside its own rules. Treat the selected checks as the scope of a run; the tool name alone does not identify that scope.

## Worked example: a null pointer constant

**Illustrative example, not run here.** With clang-tidy installed, save this C++ source as `sample.cpp`:

```cpp
int* missing_value() {
    return 0;
}
```

Select one check and supply the language standard:

```sh
clang-tidy sample.cpp '-checks=-*,modernize-use-nullptr' -- -std=c++11
```

The intended suggestion is to use `nullptr` for the returned null pointer. This command reports diagnostics without requesting automatic edits. Change `0` to `nullptr` and run it again.

## Project setup and limits

For a project, point `-p` at the directory containing its compilation database. Missing include paths, generated headers, or build definitions can prevent useful analysis.

Review fixes and run project tests before accepting them. Compare [Cppcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cppcheck/) for another native-source workflow, or [compare the three tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Fclang-tidy%2Ctools%2Fclang-static-analyzer%2Ctools%2Fcppcheck).

documents.description: Use Rust compiler-integrated lints to catch common mistakes and improve Rust code.
documents.markdown:
# Clippy

## What it does

Clippy adds lint diagnostics to Rust's compiler-based workflow. It identifies correctness mistakes, suspicious code, unnecessary complexity, and opportunities for more idiomatic or efficient code.

Its checks complement Rust's compiler errors. Passing the compiler and Clippy does not prove that application logic, unsafe code, or external interfaces behave correctly.

## Which lints run?

| Group          | How to interpret it                                                                |
| -------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Default groups | Include correctness, suspicious code, style, complexity, and performance patterns. |
| Pedantic       | Stricter checks that can be useful but may need exceptions.                        |
| Restriction    | Individual restrictions on otherwise valid code; choose rules deliberately.        |
| Nursery        | New lints still being developed.                                                   |

The project explicitly advises against enabling the whole restriction group: rules can be inappropriate for your project or conflict with one another. Choose checks based on your requirements.

## Inputs and workflow

Use Clippy with a compatible Rust toolchain and the project's Cargo workspace. The usual entry point is `cargo clippy`; workspace and package selection control the scope. Compiler-driven setup may execute build scripts or procedural macros even though the target application's runtime behavior is not being tested.

Different feature combinations or compilation targets may include different code. Keep those choices and the minimum supported Rust version with your lint configuration.

## A useful first evaluation

Start with the default lints on a representative package. Review diagnostic explanations before enabling stricter groups, then decide which warnings should fail CI. Promoting all warnings to errors also includes ordinary compiler warnings, so toolchain upgrades can affect that policy.

Some suggestions can be applied automatically. Review the resulting changes and run the project's tests rather than treating a suggested rewrite as proof that behavior is preserved.

documents.markdown: # CodeQL ## First try **Documentation reviewed on November 6, 2026; not executed here.** This builder workflow covers only Python SQL injection. Other catalog capabilities were not re-reviewed. Use the [CodeQL 2.27.4 bundle](https://github.com/github/codeql-action/releases/tag/codeql-bundle-v2.27.4) for Linux x86-64 on Ubuntu 22.04. The reviewed query pack is `codeql/python-queries@1.9.0`, with `py/sql-injection` at `Security/CWE-089/SqlInjection.ql`. The tagged query/library revision is `1be292a1e54696ca543b4ad0f9b4537b9687caa7`. 1. Check that your project is eligible under the [CLI terms](https://github.com/github/codeql-cli-binaries/blob/main/LICENSE.md). The query repository's MIT license does not replace those terms. Public-repository and private-organization entitlements differ. 2. Follow the [CLI setup guide](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/how-tos/find-and-fix-code-vulnerabilities/scan-from-the-command-line/set-up-codeql-cli). Make Python 3.12 available as `python3` and prepare the source and its dependencies. Use `codeql resolve packs` to confirm the query-pack version. 3. Choose a small Python project using modeled request sources and SQL APIs. The [upstream example](https://codeql.github.com/codeql-query-help/python/py-sql-injection/) shows Django request data reaching cursor queries. Check your framework/version and call shapes against the models; the example's legacy Django routing syntax is not a current application setup recipe. 4. Create a database without a build command, then analyze only the pinned query. In this example, `src` is your source directory and `codeql-python-db` must not already exist: ```sh codeql database create codeql-python-db --language=python --source-root=src codeql database analyze codeql-python-db codeql/python-queries@1.9.0:Security/CWE-089/SqlInjection.ql --format=sarifv2.1.0 --output=python-sql.sarif ``` The expected artifact is a SARIF file with any modeled source-to-SQL paths. Inspect extraction diagnostics first, then the source, sink, and intervening transformations. A finding calls for investigation; absence of a finding does not establish that every request path was modeled. For a confirmed string-built query, use the database API's parameter binding and rerun the same query on a fresh database. Preserve the before/after source, CLI and pack versions, extraction logs, and reports in a [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). This local result-writing command does not upload SARIF to GitHub. For another language, follow the [language-specific database preparation guide](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/tutorials/customize-code-scanning/prepare-code-for-analysis), then the [query analysis tutorial](https://docs.github.com/en/code-security/tutorials/customize-code-scanning/analyze-code). Check that language's build, host, and query requirements before reusing a Python procedure. ## Choose the question to investigate Start with the standard security checks. Use custom queries when you need to find variants of a known problem or investigate how data reaches an operation. The [query help](https://codeql.github.com/codeql-query-help/) explains individual checks and their recommendations. ## What to keep in mind Check the support matrix for the language version and framework you use. A successful database creation still needs its diagnostics reviewed for extraction problems. The CLI and the public query libraries have different licensing terms. Check the linked CLI terms before adopting it for a particular repository or service. [Understand static analysis methods](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/advanced-static-methods/#data-flow-and-taint-where-can-an-input-reach) explains what a modeled data-flow path establishes. The system builder currently uses only the Python query above; other catalog languages and query families remain outside its reviewed matching scope. ## Alternatives and complements For Java, [SpotBugs](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/spotbugs/) checks compiled class files for bug patterns, while [JBMC](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/jbmc/) checks stated properties within configured bounds. Use the [Java workflow guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/java-analysis/) to choose the input and result type that fit your task.

documents.description: Measure which Python statements and branches a test run executes.
documents.markdown:
# coverage.py

## First try

Use the [coverage fixture](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/test-evidence/#measure-execution-coverage)
to run three small unittest suites against the same Python module. It includes
exact setup and commands, declared source scope, and retained reports.

**Executed with coverage.py 7.10.6 on Windows and Python 3.13.15.** The partial
suite passed its test but left line 9 and the branch from line 3 to line 5
unexecuted. A second suite reached every line and branch without asserting any
return value. The third added assertions. These results separate execution
coverage from the strength of the checks.

## Read the report

`Missing` can name a line or a branch destination such as `3->5`. A function may
have every statement executed while still missing the false path of an `if`.
With branch measurement enabled, the combined percentage includes statements
and branch destinations; read their separate counts as well.

Keep test success, coverage collection, and a configured coverage threshold
separate. A test can pass below the threshold, or fail after executing most of
the source. Confirm that the test process completed and its data was written.
This example measures one process only.

## Use it with other testing methods

[Hypothesis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/hypothesis/) can generate inputs for properties you define.
Coverage can show which code those tests reached; it does not supply the
properties. [StrykerJS](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/strykerjs/) answers a different question for JavaScript:
whether existing tests notice selected changes to the source.

This profile is catalog-only. The system builder does not yet select a Python
test runner or a coverage collection configuration for you.

# Coverity (commercial)

## When to use it

Evaluate Coverity when you need source analysis across a mixed-language codebase and a managed review process. Establish the actual languages, compiler versions, and defect classes you want to compare before using an overall issue count as a metric.

## Worked example: review a C memory defect

**Illustrative evaluation, not run here.** In a small C project, add this function to a file included in its build:

```c
#include <stdlib.h>
void release_twice(void) {
    int *item = malloc(sizeof(*item));
    if (!item) return;
    free(item);
    free(item);
}
```

With an authorized Coverity installation:

1. Configure the C compiler and project using the installed release's instructions.
2. Capture the build and confirm the file was included.
3. Run analysis with the relevant memory checkers enabled.
4. Review any duplicate-release finding and its event path.
5. Remove the second release and compare the results.

This is an evaluation recipe, not a transcript from a licensed run. Commands and server setup depend on the installed product version.

## Commercial versus Scan

[Coverity Scan](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/coverity-scan/) has separate eligibility, listed languages, and submission limits. Use that entry when filtering for a free option.

A clean commercial scan still needs evidence that the intended code and configuration were analyzed. For C/C++ verification claims, also compare [Polyspace Code Prover](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/polyspace-code-prover/) and [Frama-C](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/frama-c/).

documents.markdown:
# Cppcheck (Open Source)

## What it does

Cppcheck examines C/C++ code for defects such as null pointer use, out-of-bounds access, uninitialized variables, and invalid memory management. Its flow-sensitive analysis tracks information about values through code. A finding can identify a correctness problem with security consequences; it does not necessarily establish an exploitable vulnerability.

## Inputs and workflow

You can analyze files directly or import a project configuration, including a compilation database. Build information helps supply the right includes and definitions. Library configuration files describe behavior that the analyzer cannot infer from a declaration alone.

The command-line tool fits local checks and continuous integration. The graphical interface provides another way to configure analysis and browse diagnostics. Findings identify the check and source location; the manual documents text and XML reporting.

## When it is useful

Consider it for native or embedded C/C++ projects, including code with platform-specific definitions. It can complement [Clang Static Analyzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/clang-static-analyzer/) because the tools use different analyses and checks.

## Coverage limits

- A different platform or set of preprocessor definitions can expose different code paths. Record which configuration was checked.
- The analyzer deliberately makes tradeoffs that can miss defects. An empty report is not a proof of correctness.
- Open-source MISRA support is partial. Premium offers additional standards coverage and compliance reporting; a tool report alone does not establish product compliance.

## A useful first evaluation

Follow the official manual to import a representative build configuration. Review configuration diagnostics before judging defect findings, then examine a small set of results with the check descriptions. Keep the analyzer version, enabled checks, exclusions, and library configuration with the report.

## Related research

**Used in a study:** The [OCPP paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf) used Cppcheck for its C and C++ implementations. The reported counts describe those projects and study configurations; they are not validated accuracy measurements or a comparison of Open Source and Premium.

See [comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/) for how to compare scope and useful findings before combining reports.
