documents.title: CVE Binary Tool (cve-bin-tool)
documents.description: Identify software components in binaries or dependency inventories and match them to known vulnerabilities.
documents.markdown:
# CVE Binary Tool (cve-bin-tool)

## What it does

CVE Binary Tool first identifies components and versions, or reads an inventory you provide. It then compares that inventory with vulnerability data to report known issues. It can also generate a software bill of materials (SBOM), which lists detected components.

This is software composition analysis (SCA). It belongs in this wiki's static section because it inspects artifacts without exercising the target application. It does not discover a new buffer overflow by reasoning about instructions as [cwe-checker](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cwe-checker/) can attempt to do.

## Inputs and ecosystem coverage

| Input                           | Examples                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Binaries and extracted packages | Signatures identify supported components, such as OpenSSL or libpng.                                                                                   |
| Dependency metadata             | Java archives or Maven metadata; JavaScript lockfiles; Python requirements and package metadata; Rust, Ruby, Go, and other documented ecosystem files. |
| Existing inventories            | Component/version lists and supported SPDX, CycloneDX, or SWID SBOMs.                                                                                  |

The language tags are a selected parser inventory. Check the manual for exact filenames, formats, and version-resolution behavior. Recognizing an archive format does not imply recognizing every component inside it.

## Reading the results

Reports associate identified components with advisories and severity information. They support human-readable and structured formats, while triage data and Vulnerability Exploitability eXchange (VEX) records can preserve reviewed decisions.

A version match is a reason to investigate. It does not demonstrate that the vulnerable functionality is reachable in your application. Component misidentification, backported fixes, missing metadata, and incomplete or stale advisory data can affect results. No findings can also mean a component was not recognized.

## A useful first evaluation

Choose a package with an independently known component inventory, update the vulnerability data, and compare the detected names and versions with that inventory. Review applicability before deciding which findings require an upgrade or mitigation.

For offline operation, prepare the database first and record its age. The manual's offline option prevents live updates; it cannot supply vulnerability records that were never downloaded.

## Related research

**Discussed in a proposed approach:** The [EV charging paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/Sheppard_CSR_2025.pdf) identifies CVE Binary Tool for compiled-code analysis in its ongoing quality-modeling work. The paper is not an accuracy evaluation of component detection or advisory matching.

[Software quality models](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/software-quality/) explains the proposed aggregation and why its conclusions depend on the available measurements. A component/advisory match retains its applicability limits when included in a broader assessment.

documents.description: Find potential weakness patterns in native binaries using Ghidra and static data flow analysis.
documents.markdown:
# cwe-checker

## What it does

The project calls its executable `cwe_checker`. It uses Ghidra to recover an intermediate representation from a binary, then applies heuristics and data flow analyses to identify potentially vulnerable code paths.

Checks cover weakness classes such as buffer errors, unsafe format strings, use after free, and null pointer dereferences. A CWE identifies a class of weakness. This tool does not work by looking up a component version in a CVE database; see [CVE Binary Tool](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cve-bin-tool/) for that workflow.

## What it can analyze

| Input                         | Documented scope                                                        |
| ----------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| ELF executables               | Main focus; examples include x86, ARM, MIPS, and PowerPC architectures. |
| Linux loadable kernel modules | Experimental; only a subset of checks runs.                             |
| Bare-metal binaries           | Experimental; requires a configuration describing the target.           |

Support in Ghidra is a prerequisite, not a guarantee that every checker fully models a particular platform. Firmware analysis still requires identifying suitable executable content and the right load configuration.

## Results and limitations

The tool produces CWE warnings, offers JSON output, and includes a Ghidra integration for reviewing findings. Use the check-specific documentation to understand each warning's assumptions and likely false positives or missed cases.

Do not equate every implemented check with default coverage: the repository explicitly notes that the command-injection check is disabled in standard runs. A warning is a lead for manual analysis, not confirmation of an exploit.

## A useful first evaluation

Use the official stable release workflow with one known ELF binary. Confirm its architecture, review enabled checks and API configuration, and inspect a warning alongside the recovered code. Record the binary hash, analyzer and Ghidra versions, and configuration for reproducibility.

## Related research

**Discussed in a paper:** [Characterizing and Codifying Malware Sophistication](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/iETC_Porcella_2026.pdf) cites cwe-checker as an example of detecting selected reliability-related weaknesses in binaries. It does not benchmark the tool or validate a malware sophistication score.

[Malware sophistication](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/binary-analysis/) connects this example to recovered-code coverage, observable features, and the limits of inferring quality from them.

documents.title: Dafny
documents.description: Verify programs written in Dafny against contracts, invariants, and other specifications.
documents.markdown:
# Dafny

## What it does

Dafny combines a programming language with a verifier. You describe expected behavior using preconditions, postconditions, assertions, loop invariants, and termination information. Verification checks whether the implementation satisfies those obligations under the stated assumptions.

It is useful for learning specification-driven development or implementing components whose properties you want to reason about explicitly.

## Specifications are part of the work

A function contract can describe what a caller must provide and what the function guarantees. Loops may need invariants that make the reasoning visible to the verifier. Proofs can require helper lemmas or more precise specifications.

A weak or mistaken specification can prove the wrong property. Verification does not substitute for deciding what the software should do.

## Interpreting failures

When a property cannot be established, examine the reported obligation, assumptions, and annotations. The implementation might be incorrect, but the verifier may also need an invariant or more solver resources. Keep timeouts and unknown results separate from demonstrated violations.

## A useful first evaluation

Follow the introductory tutorial with a small method and a precise postcondition. Try a deliberately incorrect implementation and observe the verification result, then repair it. Treat generated executable code and external integrations as additional boundaries to review and test.

documents.title: detect-secrets
documents.description: Find potential embedded secrets and review new findings against a repository baseline.
documents.markdown:
# detect-secrets

## Where it fits

detect-secrets adds a dedicated credential check to a repository. Its baseline lets a team review existing findings while checking subsequent changes.

For a review of past commits, use a history-scanning workflow such as
[Gitleaks](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/gitleaks/). See [current files and Git history](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/secret-scanning/)
to choose the scope and distinguish a review baseline from remediation.

## Review before baselining

Follow the scan and audit guides. Classify candidate findings rather than accepting a generated baseline without inspection. Keep the chosen plugins and exclusions in review with the baseline.

## First try

**Illustrative example; not executed here.** Use Python 3.12 and
[detect-secrets 1.5.0](https://pypi.org/project/detect-secrets/1.5.0/) in an isolated
environment. Install `detect-secrets==1.5.0` using the
[official setup guide](https://github.com/Yelp/detect-secrets), then record
`detect-secrets --version`. In an empty example directory, create a
`fixture` subdirectory and save `fixture/settings.py` with this dummy value:

```python
password = "violet-orchard-lantern-4829"
```

This string has no account or service behind it. Scan the file even though it is
not tracked by Git, then inspect the baseline interactively:

```sh
detect-secrets scan --all-files fixture > baseline.json
detect-secrets audit baseline.json
```

With the keyword detector enabled, expect a candidate on the assignment. The
baseline records its location, detector, and a hash; it is not proof that the
string is a valid credential. The audit step records a review decision. It does
not remove the value, revoke a credential, or make an unreviewed baseline safe.

Remove the dummy assignment and rescan to a different output file:

```sh
detect-secrets scan --all-files fixture > corrected-baseline.json
```

The candidate should be absent. If it was absent in the first scan, inspect the
enabled plugins, filters, and file scope before claiming the check is active.
For your project, retain and review the selected configuration, then follow the
[baseline audit procedure](https://github.com/Yelp/detect-secrets/blob/master/docs/audit.md).
Use synthetic strings for training; never add a real credential to test a rule.

## Handle confirmed findings

Use the affected service's process to revoke or rotate an exposed credential. Removing text from the current file alone does not undo exposure. A clean report only describes the configured scan; arbitrary secrets or excluded files can remain undetected.

# detekt

## Setup

detekt can run through its CLI or build integration. The distinction between syntax inspection and type resolution matters: knowledge of return types and symbols enables checks that a source-only parse cannot perform.

## Example

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** In a Kotlin JVM project with the detekt 1.23.8 Gradle plugin already configured, run:

```sh
./gradlew detektMain detektTest
```

On Windows, use `gradlew.bat detektMain detektTest`. These tasks analyze the main and test source sets with type resolution. The plain `detekt` task runs without type resolution in this documented configuration.

Review a finding together with its rule, source set, and analysis task. If an expected type-aware check is missing, verify the classpath and task before concluding that the rule found nothing.

## Limits

Rule selections and baselines affect visibility. Android variants and Kotlin Multiplatform projects have different generated tasks; use the matching release guide rather than copying the JVM task names unchanged.

## Related research

We used Detekt for the Kotlin implementation in our [OCPP study](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf). The study's mention of the tool does not establish that every type-aware rule was enabled. See [Comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/) for how configuration and analysis scope affect comparisons.

documents.markdown:
# .NET analyzers

## What it does

The .NET SDK includes analyzers that use compiler information to check source code. They can run during a build and in a compatible editor. The documented default enables SDK analysis for projects targeting .NET 5 or later, but the selected rules still depend on configuration and SDK version.

## Example

**Illustrative configuration, not run here.** In a C# SDK project with analysis enabled, add a rule severity to the project's `.editorconfig`:

```ini
[*.cs]
dotnet_diagnostic.CA2014.severity = warning
```

Run `dotnet build`. Rule CA2014 flags `stackalloc` inside loops because repeated stack allocation can exhaust stack space. To check the configuration, use a small method containing that construct and then a revision with allocation moved outside the loop.

Record the SDK version and effective configuration. Do not infer that every CA rule runs just because one warning appeared.

## Limits

An analyzer's finding is different from a compiler error or an IDE style suggestion. Generated code, disabled rules, and severity settings can change what a build reports. Inspect the documented rule scope when comparing results with [CodeQL](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/codeql/) or [SonarQube](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/sonarqube/).

## Related research

Our [OCPP study](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf) identifies the C# analyzer as Roslyn. That label does not establish the exact package, SDK, or rule set used. See [Comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/) for why those historical findings cannot be attributed to today's SDK defaults.

documents.title: Dr. Memory
documents.description: Detect memory errors while a compatible native executable runs under dynamic instrumentation.
documents.markdown:
# Dr. Memory

## What it does

Dr. Memory uses dynamic instrumentation to observe a native program's memory operations. It can report access to freed or unallocated memory, uninitialized reads, allocation mistakes, and selected leaks.

It executes the program. The Binaries input tag therefore describes a runtime workflow, unlike the offline inspection performed by [Ghidra](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ghidra/) or [cwe-checker](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cwe-checker/).

## Example

**Illustrative Windows workflow, not run here. No exact Windows version, architecture, and Dr. Memory release combination has been validated for this example.** The [Windows installation guide](https://drmemory.org/page_install_windows.html) covers MSI/ZIP installation and PATH setup; it does not establish an exact compatibility matrix. Check the [release information](https://github.com/DynamoRIO/drmemory/releases) and the selected package's documentation for your OS, architecture, and application before relying on this route.

Keep any debug symbols available, put the launcher on PATH, and run a local test program:

```powershell
drmemory.exe -batch -- 'C:/path/to/test-program.exe'
```

Replace the path with your executable and add its normal test arguments after it. The `-batch` option avoids automatically opening the report in a text editor. Inspect the reported results location and `results.txt`.

Reproduce a finding with the same workload. Symbols and a diagnostic-friendly build make it easier to connect a reported access to source code.

If you have source and can rebuild on native Windows x64, [Find a memory error on Windows](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/windows-memory-check/) provides a controlled MSVC AddressSanitizer experiment with a correction and an explicit validation status. It does not validate Dr. Memory compatibility.

When reading `results.txt`, identify the error category first, then the stack for the access. Where provided, compare the allocation or free stack to learn how the affected memory was created or released. Keep the report with the workload that triggered it. The [official report guide](https://drmemory.org/page_running.html) explains the output files and how to inspect a finding.

## Limits

The workload determines which paths are checked. Instrumentation changes runtime cost, and unsupported program features can complicate execution. Review stacks and suppressions before attributing a report to application code.

See [Choosing memory-error checks](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/memory-error-detection/) for comparison with [Memcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/valgrind-memcheck/) and [AddressSanitizer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/address-sanitizer/).

documents.markdown:
# ESLint

## What it does

ESLint parses source and runs configured rules to identify problematic code. Rules cover potential bugs, suspicious constructs, and coding conventions. Plugins add rules, parsers, or support for frameworks and other file types.

It is a configurable linting system. Security plugins can add useful checks, but a default ESLint run is not equivalent to a full security analysis of an application.

## JavaScript versus TypeScript

| Setup                                       | What it provides                                                                             |
| ------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| ESLint with its JavaScript parser           | JavaScript parsing and the enabled core or plugin rules.                                     |
| ESLint with typescript-eslint               | TypeScript parsing and TypeScript-specific lint rules.                                       |
| TypeScript setup with typed linting enabled | Additional rules that use TypeScript's type information, with extra setup and analysis cost. |

For example, the typescript-eslint rule set includes checks for incorrectly handled promises. The relevant rules require type information; adding a TypeScript parser alone does not enable them.

Run the [TypeScript compiler](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/typescript/) separately for project type diagnostics. Typed lint rules and `tsc --noEmit` complement each other; neither validates arbitrary runtime input.

## Inputs and results

Provide source files and a compatible Node.js environment, then configure file patterns, language options, plugins, and rules. The current configuration workflow uses an ESLint configuration file; use guidance matching your installed major version.

Findings include rule names and source locations and can appear in the terminal, an editor, or a CI report. Some rules supply automatic fixes, while others supply suggestions for a developer to review.

## A useful first evaluation

Start with the recommended configuration for your language. For TypeScript, decide whether you need type-aware rules and configure them explicitly. Inspect which files and rules actually run before making lint failures block a build.

Record plugin versions and suppressions. ESLint's capabilities depend strongly on that configuration, so two projects using ESLint may be performing different checks.

documents.title: FLOSS
documents.description: Recover ordinary and obfuscated strings from compiled programs for further investigation.
documents.markdown:
# FLOSS

## What it does

FLOSS extracts ordinary strings, strings assembled on the stack, and strings recovered from selected decoding routines. It also supports specialized extraction for Go and Rust binaries.

The project describes an advanced static-analysis workflow, but part of that workflow emulates instructions. Its [deobfuscation algorithm](https://github.com/mandiant/flare-floss/blob/master/doc/theory.md) identifies likely decoder functions, reconstructs arguments, and inspects emulator memory changes. The catalog's Static and Dynamic tags reflect these two modes.

## Example

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** Install a compatible standalone release and inspect a known test executable:

```sh
floss sample.exe
floss -j sample.exe > strings.json
```

Review a recovered string together with its type and code location. Use [Ghidra](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ghidra/) to inspect the surrounding function. A decoded path or hostname is a lead to examine, not proof that the application contacted it.

## Limits

Recovery depends on recognizing code and reproducing enough decoder behavior. Unsupported instructions, packing, environmental dependencies, or missed arguments can prevent recovery. A clean or short listing does not establish that a program contains no other strings.

For direct file-pattern matching, compare [YARA-X](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/yara-x/). For broader capability rules, compare [capa](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/capa/).

documents.title: Frama-C (Eva and WP)
documents.description: Analyze C runtime safety with Eva and verify specified C behavior with WP.
documents.markdown:
# Frama-C (Eva and WP)

## Two analyses in one framework

| Plugin | Main job                                                                | What you interpret                                                      |
| ------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Eva    | Approximate possible values and behavior using abstract interpretation. | Alarms about possible runtime errors and inferred properties.           |
| WP     | Turn annotated requirements into proof obligations.                     | Which obligations were proved, remain unknown, or need additional work. |

Eva can analyze selected classes of undefined behavior, including invalid memory access and arithmetic errors. WP supports functional specifications expressed as ACSL contracts and annotations.

## What a result means

An Eva alarm can reflect a real error or imprecision in the analysis. A failed or timed-out WP proof can reflect a false property, missing annotations, unsupported modeling, or a solver limitation. Investigate before labeling either as a confirmed bug.

Successful proofs apply to the modeled program and stated assumptions. Check the environment model, machine configuration, unsupported constructs, and trusted specifications when interpreting a result.

## Where to start

Start with a small C routine and a known environment. Use the Eva tutorial to examine value ranges and alarms, or the WP tutorial to state a function contract and inspect its obligations. Add complexity gradually and preserve annotations as part of the code review.

Frama-C also includes dynamic techniques such as E-ACSL. They have different execution requirements and should not be inferred from this entry's static tags.

See [static method results](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/advanced-static-methods/) for value approximations and proof obligations.

documents.title: Ghidra
documents.description: Recover and inspect code structure from compiled programs with disassembly and decompilation.
documents.markdown:
# Ghidra

## What it does

Ghidra helps an analyst work from machine instructions toward an understanding of a program. The listing, decompiler, function graph, and cross-references provide different views of the same artifact. Renaming functions and correcting types can improve that reconstruction.

## Example

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** Install a release and its required JDK, then launch `ghidraRun.bat` on Windows or `ghidraRun` on Linux/macOS. Create a project and import a small program you compiled yourself.

Open it in CodeBrowser, accept the relevant analysis options, and locate a function with a recognizable string. Follow its references and compare the decompiler view with the source and disassembly. Keep the executable and build settings with your notes.

## Limits

Decompiled output is a reconstruction, not the original source. Stripped symbols, optimization, indirect calls, and obfuscation can obscure structure. A plausible function name or type still needs supporting evidence.

For predefined weakness checks, see [cwe-checker](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cwe-checker/). For a programmable path exploration workflow, see [angr](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/angr/).

## Related research

In our [malware sophistication paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/iETC_Porcella_2026.pdf), we discuss Ghidra in the context of binary analysis and obfuscation. We did not benchmark its detection performance. [Malware sophistication](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/binary-analysis/) explains how recovered structure affects the interpretation of software quality.

documents.title: Gitleaks (Git history)
documents.description: Find candidate secrets in the patches of a local Git repository.
documents.markdown:
# Gitleaks (Git history)

## Where it fits

Use Gitleaks for a history investigation. Use [detect-secrets](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/detect-secrets/)
for its reviewed current-file baseline and prevention workflow. The
[secret-scanning guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/secret-scanning/) explains how their scopes
and follow-up actions differ.

Gitleaks is in maintenance mode: its current project notice promises security
patches, not new features. This entry documents version 8.30.1; it does not
substitute Betterleaks commands or capabilities.

## First try

**Illustrative procedure, not executed here.** Install the official 8.30.1 binary
for your host and check `gitleaks version`. Use Git 2.28 or later and a Linux
shell in a new scratch directory. This example creates a repository with no
remote and a dummy token that cannot authenticate anywhere.

Create a rule outside the repository. It detects only the synthetic marker:

```toml
# Save as demo-rule.toml.
title = "Synthetic history check"
[[rules]]
id = "demo-only-token"
description = "Synthetic fixture marker"
regex = '''DEMO_ONLY_[A-Z0-9]+'''
```

Record the marker, then replace it in a second commit:

```sh
git init -b main secret-history-demo
printf '%s\n' 'demo_token = "DEMO_ONLY_0123456789"' > secret-history-demo/settings.txt
git -C secret-history-demo add settings.txt
git -C secret-history-demo -c user.name=Demo -c user.email=demo@example.invalid commit -m "Add dummy marker"
printf '%s\n' 'demo_token = "REMOVED"' > secret-history-demo/settings.txt
git -C secret-history-demo add settings.txt
git -C secret-history-demo -c user.name=Demo -c user.email=demo@example.invalid commit -m "Remove dummy marker"
git -C secret-history-demo rev-parse HEAD
gitleaks git secret-history-demo --log-opts="HEAD" --config demo-rule.toml --redact=100 --report-format json --report-path history.json --exit-code 10
```

The scan covers commits reachable from this repository's `HEAD`. It uses the
single custom rule, no baseline, and no intentional exclusions. Run it from a
scratch directory without a `.gitleaksignore` file. The expected report contains
`demo-only-token` for `settings.txt` in the first commit; configured status `10`
indicates findings. A command error or incomplete scan is not a clean result.

Removing the value from the current file does not remove its earlier patch.
Keep `history.json`, the rule, the recorded `HEAD`, and the command in a
[run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). Redaction reduces value exposure; still
inspect reports before sharing because paths, identities, and commit context
can be sensitive.

## Use a real repository

Choose the refs and range deliberately. A shallow clone or a clone missing
remote refs cannot supply history it does not contain. Record fetch depth,
selected refs, rules, allowlists, baseline, and limits with the result. A
baseline hides matching earlier findings; it does not remediate them.

This entry is catalog-only. Source files alone do not establish that the
builder has the repository history needed for this workflow.

# Go race detector

## Where it fits

The race detector examines executions involving goroutines and shared memory. Pair it with [go vet](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/go-vet/) and normal behavior tests.

## Use a representative workload

Follow the guide's race-enabled test or build workflow. Confirm the selected platform's cgo and compiler requirements first. Tests must reach the shared-state operations for the detector to observe them.

## Preserve a reproducer

Use both conflicting-access traces to understand a report. Add a test that exercises the failure after fixing synchronization. Budget for instrumentation overhead, and treat a clean run as evidence about that workload rather than all possible executions.

# gosec

## Where it fits

Use gosec alongside [Staticcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/staticcheck/) when reviewing Go: their selected checks and intended emphasis differ. Start with the same module revision and build configuration so a comparison does not accidentally scan different packages.

## Worked example: a module report

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** With a compatible Go toolchain and gosec installed, run in the module directory:

```sh
gosec -fmt json -out gosec-results.json ./...
```

Open `gosec-results.json` and inspect an issue's rule, severity, confidence, and code location. A useful trial is a small project containing a TLS client configured to skip certificate verification, followed by a corrected version. Treat any finding as something to investigate in the application's context.

## Coverage and exclusions

Confirm packages loaded successfully before interpreting a low issue count. Document build tags, selected rules, and exclusions with the result. An inline suppression can conceal a real problem if its scope is too broad.

A nonzero exit can reflect findings or a processing error. A zero exit under a configured no-fail option is not evidence that the scan found nothing. These details matter when interpreting CI results.

Dependency advisory matching is a separate job; see [OSV-Scanner](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/osv-scanner/).

## Related research

**Used in a study:** The [OCPP paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf) used gosec as its Go-specific analyzer alongside SonarQube and Semgrep. The study examined one Go implementation and did not validate finding accuracy.

[Comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/) explains why successful execution, rule scope, and project context matter when interpreting such counts.

documents.title: Hypothesis
documents.description: Generate Python test inputs and simplify failing examples for properties you define.
documents.markdown: # Hypothesis ## What it does You write a test that should hold for many inputs and describe those inputs using strategies. Hypothesis generates examples, runs the test, and tries to simplify a failure into a smaller example that remains useful for debugging. For example, a serialization test might assert that decoding an encoded value recovers the original value. A generated edge case can reveal a broken assumption that a few handwritten examples miss. ## Properties and strategies The property defines what is correct; the strategy defines which inputs are explored. A test that only checks that no exception occurs will miss incorrect results that return normally. Overly restrictive strategies can exclude important cases. Hypothesis works with ordinary Python testing workflows and also supports stateful tests. Stateful operation sequences are different from automatically understanding a physical system's temporal-logic specification. ## Interpreting results A failing example demonstrates that the test failed for that execution. Investigate whether the problem is in the implementation, the property, or the test setup. Repeatability matters: hidden state and flaky external behavior can interfere with replay and shrinking. A passing run covers the examples exercised within its configured budget; it is not a proof over every possible input. [coverage.py](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/coverage-py/) can measure which Python lines and branches the test run reaches. It does not judge whether the property is strong enough. The [test-evidence guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/test-evidence/) compares execution coverage, source mutation, and generated inputs. ## First try **Illustrative example; not executed here.** Use Python 3.13 with [Hypothesis 6.168.0](https://pypi.org/project/hypothesis/6.168.0/) in an isolated environment on Windows, Linux, or macOS. Follow the [quickstart](https://hypothesis.readthedocs.io/en/latest/quickstart.html), installing `hypothesis==6.168.0`. Save this as `test_magnitude.py`: ```python from hypothesis import given, strategies as st def magnitude(value: int) -> int: return value @given(st.integers(min_value=-100, max_value=100)) def test_nonnegative(value: int) -> None: assert magnitude(value) >= 0 if __name__ == "__main__": test_nonnegative() ``` Run the test directly; no separate test runner is needed: ```sh python test_magnitude.py ``` Expect an assertion failure with a negative generated input. Hypothesis attempts to simplify the failing example; do not depend on a particular discovery order. Replace `return value` with `return abs(value)` and rerun. The selected property should then hold for the examples generated in this run. This property checks only nonnegativity. A function that always returns zero would also satisfy it, so add properties that express your actual contract, such as agreement with a trusted reference or a round trip. Keep the failing example as a regression test, and record the Hypothesis version, strategies, settings, and any example database needed for replay in the [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/).

documents.description: Find memory and value errors across function calls using Infer's Pulse analysis.
documents.markdown:
# Infer (Pulse)

## When to use it

Use Pulse to investigate errors that involve calls between functions, such as a value becoming null before another function dereferences it. It complements the pattern and rule workflows in [Semgrep CE](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/semgrep-ce/).

Capturing the real build matters. A missing compilation unit or an unmodeled library changes the program the analyzer sees. Infer's capture step is preparation for static analysis, even when it invokes a compiler.

## Worked example: a definite null dereference

**Illustrative example, not run here.** With Infer and a compatible Clang installed, save this as `null_access.c`:

```c
int read_value(void) {
    int *value = 0;
    return *value;
}
```

Run the capture and analysis:

```sh
infer run --pulse -- clang -c null_access.c
```

Inspect the report for a null-dereference diagnostic at `*value`. Then give the pointer a valid object and compare the result. The diagnostic demonstrates one selected check; it does not measure coverage across your application.

## Interpret a clean result

Pulse can retain an issue until a caller establishes the conditions needed to report it. It also models missing functions with assumptions. Review capture failures, skipped code, and external models before treating silence as evidence.

For runtime alternatives, see [memory-error detection](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/memory-error-detection/).

documents.description: Check Java bytecode for runtime exceptions and assertion violations using bounded model checking.
documents.markdown:
# JBMC

## What it examines

JBMC consumes compiled classes and models their behavior. It does not infer a complete application contract from the source. [SpotBugs](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/spotbugs/) also reads bytecode, but applies defect detectors rather than this bounded-verification workflow.

## Worked example: an array bounds violation

**Illustrative example, not run here.** Save `BoundsCheck.java`:

```java
public class BoundsCheck {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        int[] values = new int[2];
        values[2] = 7;
    }
}
```

Compile with a JDK whose class-file version your JBMC release supports:

```sh
javac BoundsCheck.java
```

On a Unix-style host, replace `JBMC_MODELS` with the path to the matching `core-models.jar`, then run:

```sh
jbmc BoundsCheck --unwind 5 --classpath "JBMC_MODELS:."
```

Use the host's classpath separator when adapting the command. Look for a failed array-access or exception property. Interpret the property report rather than relying only on the overall exit status.

## Bounds and environment

A check limited to a number of loop iterations does not automatically cover longer behavior. The classpath and runtime-library models also determine which behavior is represented.

Compare results only after matching the entry point, properties, and assumptions. See [Java source and bytecode analysis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/java-analysis/).

documents.title: Grafana k6 OSS
documents.description: Exercise an HTTP service with a defined workload and evaluate response metrics against explicit thresholds.
documents.markdown:
# Grafana k6 OSS

## First try

Use the repository's
[`examples/http-api`](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/http-api)
fixture and k6 1.0.0. The [local API guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/api-testing/)
describes its loopback service. From the fixture directory, start the corrected
service in one terminal:

```sh
python server.py --fixed
```

In another terminal in that directory, run the supplied script:

```sh
k6 run --no-usage-report load.js
```

The script accepts only an IPv4 loopback URL. Its default endpoint is
`http://127.0.0.1:8771/health`; `BASE_URL` can select another loopback port.
Setup requires the fixture's `ready` status and `fixed` mode before starting
load. This read-only endpoint needs no authentication, test data, or reset.
Stop the server with Ctrl+C afterward.

The workload uses two virtual users for ten seconds, with a half-second pause
after each request. This is a closed model: slower iterations reduce the arrival
rate. It is not a fixed requests-per-second target. Each load request has a
two-second timeout and the scenario allows two seconds to finish at the end.

The selected criteria are all response checks passing, no failed HTTP requests,
and the 95th-percentile load-request duration below 500 ms. These are tutorial
thresholds, not a service-level objective for your project. The script saves
`k6-summary.json`; preserve it under a new name before another run.

## Separate checks, thresholds, and completion

Checks record Boolean outcomes. Without a corresponding threshold, failed
checks do not make the whole run fail. Inspect the process status, completed
iterations, and threshold results together. If setup fails before load, empty
metrics or apparently passing thresholds are not a successful measurement.

**Executed on Windows with k6 1.0.0 against the local fixture.** A run completed
40 load iterations with its thresholds met. A deliberately impossible latency
threshold failed while response checks passed. The faulty-mode service failed
setup before load. These are checks of the recipe and status handling, not
service-capacity measurements. The
[execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/audits/remaining-work/executions/k6/record.json)
retains input hashes, commands, endpoint ports, and process statuses beside the
captured summaries.

## Adapt the workload

Record the target revision, service settings, generator host, competing activity,
network path, duration, arrival model, and thresholds in a
[run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). Prepare reset and cleanup before testing
operations that change data. Use the load model appropriate to the intended
demand and check that the generator can produce it.

[Schemathesis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/schemathesis/) generates schema-based requests;
[RESTler](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/restler/) explores stateful API sequences. k6 evaluates your chosen
workload and thresholds. These tools answer different questions.

documents.description: Check Rust safety properties and assertions with model checking and explicit proof harnesses.
documents.markdown:
# Kani

## Where it fits

Kani lets you express a claim about a Rust function and ask whether the modeled inputs satisfy it. [Clippy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/clippy/) instead provides a catalog of lint checks. Both can be useful on the same crate.

## Worked example: challenge a property

**Illustrative example, not run here.** With Kani installed and set up, create a library crate and place this harness in `src/lib.rs`:

```rust
#[cfg(kani)]
#[kani::proof]
fn increment_always_increases() {
    let value: u8 = kani::any();
    let next = value.saturating_add(1);
    assert!(next > value);
}
```

Run from the crate root:

```sh
cargo kani
```

The assertion is false for `value == 255`: saturation leaves the value unchanged. Inspect the failed property and counterexample. Changing the property to `next >= value` expresses a different, valid claim for this example.

## Avoid proving the wrong problem

An assumption can exclude the failing value. That only helps if the real caller actually satisfies the assumption. Record the input domain and explain its connection to the application's contract.

Loops, external behavior, and unsupported Rust features require additional modeling. A timeout or unresolved analysis is not a successful proof.

See [verification and generated tests](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/verification-and-generated-tests/) for the distinction from property-based testing.

# libFuzzer

## What it does

libFuzzer repeatedly passes generated inputs to a target function inside the same process. Instrumentation reports coverage, helping it retain inputs that explore new behavior. Sanitizers can provide additional error detection.

## When it is useful

Consider it for a parser, decoder, or library routine that accepts input bytes. A small harness makes that routine accessible to the fuzzer.

## What to keep in mind

The harness defines what gets exercised. It needs to handle repeated calls, and the target should not terminate the process for ordinary invalid input. A crash is a starting point for investigation, not automatically a security vulnerability.

The project documents continued important bug fixes but no expectation of major new features. Check its status when choosing an engine for new work.

## Getting started

Follow the official tutorial to build a harness and a small input corpus. Preserve reproducible failures as regression cases.

documents.description: Inspect an Android APK for manifest, permission, certificate, and selected code-security findings.
documents.markdown:
# MobSF (Android APK static analysis)

## Where it fits

MobSF adds package-level evidence beside source checks such as
[detekt](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/detekt/). Use [Ghidra](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ghidra/) when a finding needs manual native
code investigation. This static scan does not run the Android app.

## First try

**Illustrative procedure, not executed here.** Use an APK you built and may
inspect. Record its build revision and SHA-256 digest. The example assumes a
local Linux Docker Engine 28 or later, default bridge/NAT networking, and an
available `8000` host port.

Pull the versioned image and record the resolved digest:

```sh
docker pull opensecurity/mobile-security-framework-mobsf:v4.6.4
docker image inspect --format '{{json .RepoDigests}}' opensecurity/mobile-security-framework-mobsf:v4.6.4
docker run --name mobsf-apk-review --rm -it \
  -p 127.0.0.1:8000:8000 \
  -e MOBSF_DOMAIN_MALWARE_SCAN=0 \
  opensecurity/mobile-security-framework-mobsf:v4.6.4
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8000`, use the documented initial login `mobsf/mobsf`, and
upload your APK to this local instance. Keep authentication enabled. This
procedure disables domain-malware enrichment and otherwise uses the release's
default static settings. Record any changes, skipped analyses, and timeouts.

The explicit loopback binding matters: visiting a loopback URL does not make an
all-interface listener private. Older Docker releases and nondefault routing
need separate network review. Local hosting also does not establish offline
operation; image setup and enabled features may use the network.

## Interpret the report

First check the package identity and whether analysis completed. Representative
sections include certificate information, requested permissions, manifest
issues, and code findings. A permission can be necessary for the app's purpose;
trace a reported issue to its manifest setting or code before assigning a fix.
Sections may be absent or incomplete for a particular APK.

Save the report, APK digest, image digest, and settings in the
[run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). After a justified source or build change,
build a new APK and compare the corresponding finding. Do not treat a higher
score as proof that the application is secure. Save needed reports before
stopping the temporary container with `docker stop mobsf-apk-review` from another
terminal.

This entry stays outside automatic matching because the builder does not yet
model APK artifacts. Selecting Native executable or Other is not a substitute.

documents.title: mypy
documents.description: Check Python types to find incompatible arguments, return values, and operations without running the program.
documents.markdown: # mypy ## Where it fits Use mypy to check whether code uses the types described by annotations and stubs consistently. It complements [Ruff](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ruff/) for linting and [Bandit](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/bandit/) for selected Python security patterns. A clean lint run is not a type-checking result. Gradual typing lets a project adopt annotations in stages. By default, bodies of functions without annotations receive limited checking. `Any` and ignored imports can also let type mistakes pass unnoticed. ## First try **Illustrative example, not run here.** Follow the [mypy installation instructions](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/getting_started.html) in your selected Python environment, then save this as `sample.py`: ```python def next_count(count: int) -> int: return count + 1 next_count("three") ``` Check it without running the program: ```sh python -m mypy sample.py ``` Representative diagnostic, not captured output (formatting varies by version): ```text sample.py:4: error: Argument 1 to "next_count" has incompatible type "str"; expected "int" [arg-type] ``` `sample.py:4` locates the call. `arg-type` identifies an incompatible argument type: text was passed to an integer parameter. Replace the argument with `3` and check again. This example exercises one mismatch, not the entire type system. See the [argument-type diagnostic reference](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/error_code_list.html#check-argument-types-arg-type) for details. Use the [shared Ruff and mypy recipe](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/python-checks/) for a pinned environment, faulty/corrected files, and separate reports. ## Configure a useful check Supply the project's imports and any required third-party stubs. Start with a small annotated area, inspect errors, and tighten the configuration deliberately. `--check-untyped-defs` can inspect unannotated bodies, while `--strict` enables a broader set of checks. Record the mypy version, configuration, target Python version, and suppressions. Static types do not validate arbitrary input data at runtime or replace application tests. [Compare mypy, Ruff, and Bandit](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Fmypy%2Ctools%2Fruff%2Ctools%2Fbandit) to see their different roles. ## Compare Python type checkers [Pyright](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/pyright/) is another Python type checker. Both use annotations and stubs, but configuration, inference, diagnostics, and plugin support differ. For a useful trial, check the same revision with matching Python version, platform, imports, and intended strictness. Investigate disagreements instead of comparing diagnostic counts. Keep [mypy import and stub settings](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/running_mypy.html) and [Pyright settings](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/main/docs/configuration.md) with the reports. [Compare mypy and Pyright](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Fmypy%2Ctools%2Fpyright). Ruff remains complementary for lint rules; running two type checkers is a deliberate evaluation choice, not a requirement of the Python recipe.

documents.description: Match project dependencies and supported container artifacts against known vulnerability records.
documents.markdown:
# OSV-Scanner

## What it examines

OSV-Scanner identifies dependencies and looks them up in vulnerability data. Its source scanning command refers to scanning a project directory; it does not imply the same code-behavior analysis as [CodeQL](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/codeql/).

Image scanning extracts supported installed artifacts. It is static inspection of the image, not a test of a running container.

[Trivy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/trivy/) provides another package-vulnerability workflow and separate infrastructure-configuration checks. [Compare Trivy and OSV-Scanner](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Ftrivy%2Ctools%2Fosv-scanner) without treating their input and scanner coverage as identical.

## Worked example: inspect a dependency inventory

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** With OSV-Scanner v2 installed, enter a project with a supported lockfile, such as `pnpm-lock.yaml` or `Cargo.lock`:

```sh
osv-scanner scan source --format json --output-file osv-results.json -r .
```

Review the identified package, version, ecosystem, and advisory identifiers. A result means the identified version matches the advisory conditions; investigate whether the affected behavior is used. The exact findings change with the lockfile and advisory database.

For an image workflow, replace `IMAGE_REFERENCE` with a specific image you intend to inspect:

```sh
osv-scanner scan image IMAGE_REFERENCE
```

Prefer recording its immutable digest with the result.

## Limits and comparisons

A resolved lockfile is generally more precise about selected versions than an unpinned manifest. Missing inventories or unsupported extractors can leave dependencies invisible. Updating advisory data can change results without changing your software.

Compare [CVE Binary Tool](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cve-bin-tool/) when your starting point is embedded component identification. Keep component detection accuracy separate from advisory matching, and distinguish a scan error from a clean report.

Use the [finding review workflow](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/) to investigate advisory matches. Check the [execution and data boundaries](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/execution-and-data/) before choosing local, connected, or offline use.

documents.title: PHPStan
documents.description: Use PHP types, declarations, and inference to find incorrect calls, invalid access, and other code errors.
documents.markdown:
# PHPStan

## What it does

PHPStan reasons about PHP code using declarations, inferred types, and PHPDoc annotations. Depending on the chosen rule level, it can report undefined symbols, incompatible arguments or return values, invalid member access, and unsafe use of nullable or mixed values.

Its focus is code correctness through static analysis. A clean PHPStan report does not establish that an application is free of injection flaws or other security defects.

## Inputs and setup

Supply your source, PHPStan configuration, and enough dependency information for symbol discovery. Composer installations, stubs, and framework extensions help the analyzer understand libraries and dynamically supplied behavior.

The analyzer's own PHP runtime requirement differs from the PHP version targeted by the application. Set the intended target and consult the requirements of the installed release.

## Rule levels and gradual adoption

Rule levels increase the strictness of analysis. Type hints and accurate PHPDoc give stricter checks more useful information; inaccurate annotations can also make results misleading.

A baseline records existing errors so later checks can focus on new ones. It is useful for adopting analysis in a large codebase, but the recorded errors remain unresolved. Treat the baseline as maintained analysis scope rather than evidence that those errors are harmless.

## When it is useful

Consider it for a PHP application undergoing refactoring, stricter typing, or framework upgrades. For example, changing a method's accepted type can expose incompatible callers before they are reached by tests.

## A useful first evaluation

Follow the official Composer-based setup, analyze your own source directories, and resolve missing-symbol configuration before judging the findings. Choose a rule level you can review, then raise it as type information improves. Keep extensions, target PHP version, and baseline changes under version control.

documents.title: PMD
documents.description: Apply language-specific rules to find coding defects and maintainability problems across several source languages.
documents.markdown:
# PMD

## What it does

PMD parses source code and applies a configured set of rules. Depending on the language and ruleset, findings can cover suspicious constructs, unused code, error handling, complexity, and maintainability. Rules can be extended through Java or XPath.

Java and Salesforce Apex are major use cases. Other supported languages have their own rule inventories; selecting a language does not promise equivalent detection depth across all languages.

## PMD versus CPD

| Component             | Main job                           | Language caveat                                                                     |
| --------------------- | ---------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| PMD rule analysis     | Report violations of coding rules. | Use the rule reference for the chosen language.                                     |
| CPD, bundled with PMD | Find repeated code fragments.      | Its larger language list includes languages that do not have PMD bug-finding rules. |

For example, CPD's C++ support does not make PMD a C++ defect analyzer. Likewise, parser support alone is insufficient: the documentation lists Scala parsing but no supplied Scala rules. These cases are excluded from this entry's language tags.

## Inputs and results

Provide source files, a compatible Java runtime for PMD, a language configuration, and a ruleset. Java analysis may also need an auxiliary classpath for dependencies so type resolution has the right information.

You can run PMD from its command line or through build integrations such as Maven and Gradle. Reports identify violated rules and source locations. Keep rule priorities, exclusions, and suppressions with the results.

## A useful first evaluation

Choose one language and inspect its available rules before adopting a ruleset. Run it on representative source, review several findings, and adjust rules that do not express your project's requirements. A quality gate based on rule violations is a configured policy, not a proof that all defects have been found.

documents.description: Use abstract interpretation to prove selected C and C++ runtime checks safe or identify possible and definite failures.
documents.markdown:
# Polyspace Code Prover

## What it establishes

Code Prover examines a configured model of C/C++ behavior and classifies selected runtime checks. Its goal differs from simply collecting suspicious code patterns. [Frama-C Eva](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/frama-c/) is another useful reference for understanding abstract-interpretation results.

A result about generated C code is a result about that code and configuration. It is not a general proof about a Simulink controller's temporal requirements.

## Worked example: a division precondition

**Illustrative evaluation, not run here.** Add this C function to a licensed Code Prover project:

```c
int quotient(int denominator) {
    return 12 / denominator;
}
```

Configure it as an analyzed entry point with an input domain that includes zero, then inspect the division check. It cannot be established safe for that entire domain. The exact result presentation depends on the analysis setup.

Now constrain the input to positive values and repeat. A safe result under that restriction requires evidence that the real callers enforce it. Alternatively, implement and analyze a guard for zero.

## Read the result categories

Distinguish checks proved safe, checks proved to fail, unreachable code, and checks left unproven. An unproven result may require a code fix, better environment modeling, or more precise analysis.

Record target integer sizes, stubs, ranges, and excluded code with the report. For a concrete execution-based comparison, see [memory-error detection](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/memory-error-detection/).

documents.markdown:
# Psalm

## What it does

Psalm uses inferred types and annotations to examine PHP code. Its security mode follows data from modeled untrusted sources toward sensitive operations, including output and database sinks.

Compare [PHPStan](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/phpstan/) for another PHP type-analysis workflow. Similar language coverage does not mean identical rules or framework models.

## Example

**Illustrative workflow, not run here.** In a PHP project with Composer configured:

```sh
composer require --dev vimeo/psalm
vendor/bin/psalm --init
vendor/bin/psalm --no-cache
```

Review the generated `psalm.xml` and its included paths. For the separate security workflow, run:

```sh
vendor/bin/psalm --taint-analysis
```

Inspect the reported path and the expected escaping or validation at its sink. A sanitizer appropriate for one output context may not be appropriate for another.

## Limits

Dynamic behavior and missing models can affect results. Suppressions and baselines change which issues are visible; retain them with the report. A successful ordinary run is not evidence that the separate taint mode checked the project.

## Related research

We used Psalm for the PHP implementation in our [OCPP study](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf). The paper does not establish that we enabled its separate taint-analysis mode. See [Comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/) for the distinction between current capabilities and the reported study configuration.

See [static method results](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/advanced-static-methods/) for data-flow and taint interpretation.

documents.title: PSScriptAnalyzer
documents.description: Review PowerShell scripts and modules with selected static-analysis rules.
documents.markdown:
# PSScriptAnalyzer

## First try

**Executed on Windows with PowerShell 7.6.9 and PSScriptAnalyzer 1.25.0.** The faulty file produced one `PSAvoidUsingWriteHost` warning at line 2; the corrected file produced none. The target scripts were not run.

Install the selected module into your user scope and import that version:

```powershell
Install-Module PSScriptAnalyzer -RequiredVersion 1.25.0 -Scope CurrentUser
Import-Module PSScriptAnalyzer -RequiredVersion 1.25.0
```

Save this as `greeting.ps1`:

```powershell
function Get-Greeting {
    Write-Host 'Hello, Ada'
}
```

Inspect the file with the named rule, without `-Fix`:

```powershell
Invoke-ScriptAnalyzer -Path ./greeting.ps1 -IncludeRule PSAvoidUsingWriteHost |
    Select-Object RuleName, Severity, Line, Message
```

The diagnostic asks whether display-only output is appropriate. To return this function's greeting through the pipeline, replace `Write-Host` with `Write-Output` and repeat the check. A deliberate display function can have a different design; the rule is not a claim that every `Write-Host` use is a defect.

The repository retains the pair in [`examples/powershell-check`](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/powershell-check). Use explicit `-IncludeRule` or a reviewed settings file as you expand the check.

## Interpret records before choosing a CI gate

Ordinary command completion does not mean that no diagnostics were returned. Inspect the returned records and execution errors separately. `-EnableExit` terminates the PowerShell session and uses the number of error records for its status; it is not a general gate for every warning. Define which severities and rules block your change, and retain the records with the [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/).

## Related checks

[ShellCheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/shellcheck/) covers Bourne-style shell languages, not PowerShell. A general [secret scanner](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/detect-secrets/) can complement either source analyzer, with its own candidate-review and exposure-response workflow.

documents.title: PSY-TaLiRo
documents.description: Use a Python harness to search for system behaviors that violate temporal requirements.
documents.markdown: # PSY-TaLiRo ## What it does PSY-TaLiRo connects a model, a requirement evaluator, and an optimizer. The model turns inputs into a timed trace; the evaluator scores that trace; the search tries further inputs to find a requirement violation. It follows the S-TaLiRo approach in a separate Python toolbox. Its interfaces support different simulation and monitoring backends. ## When it is useful Consider it for a Python-based experiment or a simulator you can call from Python. A model wrapper exposes the signals needed to assess the requirement. ## Temporal requirements The documentation demonstrates STL monitoring with RTAMT. Formula syntax, time semantics, and supported operators depend on the selected monitor. Choose that backend before translating a requirement into a formula. ## What to keep in mind Search quality depends on the input bounds, simulation, score, and budget. Preserve the input, trace, random seed, and configuration when a test fails. A completed search without a violation is not a proof of correctness. ## First try **Documentation-led procedure; not executed here.** Use Python 3.12 in an isolated environment with `psy-taliro==3.1.0`; the [release metadata](https://github.com/cpslab-asu/psy-taliro/blob/v3.1.0/pyproject.toml) specifies Python and dependency requirements. Follow the [installation guide](https://psy-taliro.readthedocs.io/latest/installation.html). 1. Save the complete [3.1.0 nonlinear ODE example](https://github.com/cpslab-asu/psy-taliro/blob/v3.1.0/examples/nonlinear.py) as `nonlinear.py`. It supplies the model, RTAMT formula, input bounds, optimizer, and budget. 2. For an analysis-only first run, remove the Plotly import and the plotting code after `min_eval = ...`. Add `print(min_eval.cost, min_eval.inputs.static)` there instead. Set `seed=0` in `TestOptions` and record it. 3. Run `python nonlinear.py`. A completed run returns evaluations; inspect the lowest cost, its sampled initial conditions, and `min_eval.extra.trace`. A dependency or monitor failure is not a completed search. 4. Interpret the cost under this RTAMT formula: a negative robustness value is evidence of a violation in the evaluated trace. Preserve and replay that input before changing the model. A nonnegative minimum from a finite search does not establish universal satisfaction. Use the [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/) to retain the model, formula, seed, budget, sampled input, and trace. When adapting the example, first verify the signals, units, and time semantics against your requirement. Change the model or an incorrect assumption, then compare the same scenario and repeat the search. Read [model and temporal falsification](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/model-falsification/) for the distinction between replay and search.

# PVS-Studio

## What it does

PVS-Studio analyzes source for programming errors and potential security weaknesses. The vendor describes a combination of pattern checks, data flow analysis, type information, and other semantic analyses. Individual diagnostics can be mapped to weakness classifications or coding standards.

Typical examples include invalid pointer or reference use, incorrect conditions, and suspicious value handling. Read the language-specific diagnostic explanation to determine what a finding establishes.

## Inputs and integrations

Supply source and the build or project information required by the selected analyzer. For C/C++, compiler settings determine which headers, macros, and platform definitions are analyzed. A compilation database or supported build integration can provide that context.

The product supports local and CI workflows, IDE integrations, and report exports. The exact workflow differs for C/C++, .NET, JVM, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Go projects; check the documentation for the chosen language and build system.

## When it is useful

Consider it when you want a commercial analyzer with support and several language families, especially when compiler compatibility or integration with an existing build system matters. Compare it with [Cppcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/cppcheck/) for C/C++ work and [SonarQube Server](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/sonarqube/) for broader project review workflows.

## What to keep in mind

A diagnostic's CWE or coding-standard mapping describes its classification, not complete coverage of that standard. Rules, target platforms, and dependencies need review for each project. Suppressing existing findings changes what reviewers see; it does not resolve the underlying issues.

The free open-source program has narrower eligibility than simply having a public repository. Confirm the current terms for your project before relying on free access.

## A useful first evaluation

Choose a representative project and the matching analyzer integration. Review a small set of findings against the diagnostic reference, then assess the paid or eligible free license against the platforms and workflow features you need. Record your configuration and exclusions when comparing results with another tool.

# py-spy

## First try

**Illustrative profiling procedure, not executed here.** Use Linux x86\_64 and
CPython 3.12. Run from the repository's
[`examples/py-spy`](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/py-spy)
directory. Its bounded workload repeatedly performs a named calculation and
uses no external service or application data.

Create an isolated environment and record a ten-second window at 100 samples
per second:

```sh
python3.12 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/python -m pip install py-spy==0.4.3
.venv/bin/py-spy --version
.venv/bin/py-spy record --duration 10 --rate 100 --format flamegraph --output profile.svg -- .venv/bin/python workload.py --seconds 15
```

The sampler launches the child interpreter. This can avoid Linux's usual
restriction on attaching to a non-child process, but the host must still allow
process-memory reads. If recording fails with a permission or setup error,
record that failure; it is not evidence that the workload has no hot path.
Use an environment whose policy permits the operation instead of disabling
system-wide protections.

Open `profile.svg` locally. Look for `busy_work` and inspect the sample share of
its call path. Record the actual sample count, duration, workload revision,
interpreter, and command in a [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). Sampling
errors or an early target exit can make the recording incomplete. Do not infer
an exact execution count or speedup from flame-graph width.

## Choose the output you need

| Command  | Output                                   | Useful question                                     |
| -------- | ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------- |
| `record` | A saved profile over an interval         | Which call paths dominated these samples?           |
| `top`    | A changing live function summary         | Where is this workload spending time now?           |
| `dump`   | A current stack snapshot for each thread | Where is this process currently stopped or running? |

An attached `dump` is a different permission case from the launch-under-profiler
example. Its optional local-variable output can contain application data.
Keep it off unless you need it and can handle that data appropriately.

Change one suspected source of cost, repeat the same workload, and compare
timings as well as profiles. Sampling identifies where to investigate; it does
not by itself show that a change preserved behavior or will help another load.

This entry is catalog-only because the builder does not model process-inspection
permission. Python plus Running applications is not enough to establish it.

documents.description: Inspect Python source for selected programming mistakes, conventions, and maintainability issues.
documents.markdown:
# Pylint

## Where it fits

Use Pylint when reviewing Python conventions and inferred code behavior. Compare its messages with [Ruff](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ruff/), and use [mypy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/mypy/) or [Pyright](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/pyright/) for a dedicated type-checking workflow.

## Start with a small package

The official [installation guide](https://pylint.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user_guide/installation/command_line_installation.html)
and [run instructions](https://pylint.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user_guide/usage/run.html)
cover setup and configuration. For a first result on Windows, use Python 3.13
and Pylint 4.1.3 with the shared greeting example.

[Get the examples](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/get-examples/), then enter the example directory
from the downloaded repository's root and check your interpreter:

```powershell
Set-Location examples/python-checks
$Python = "python"
& $Python --version
```

Expect `Python 3.13.x`. If needed, set `$Python` to your installed Python 3.13
executable, such as `$Python = "C:\path\to\Python313\python.exe"`, and repeat
the check. Create the environment if you have not already created it for this
example, then install the pinned release:

```powershell
& $Python -m venv .venv
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pip install pylint==4.1.3
```

Check only `unused-import` (`W0611`) so the correction has one clear result:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pylint --rcfile=pyproject.toml --disable=all `
  --enable=unused-import --score=n --persistent=n bad/greeting.py
$LASTEXITCODE
```

Expect `W0611: Unused import math (unused-import)` and exit code `4`, indicating
a warning. The supplied correction removes that import. Check it with the same
options:

```powershell
.\.venv\Scripts\python.exe -m pylint --rcfile=pyproject.toml --disable=all `
  --enable=unused-import --score=n --persistent=n good/greeting.py
$LASTEXITCODE
```

Expect no diagnostics and exit code `0`. This is an isolated message check;
the explicit fixture config and command options keep its scope small. Normal
project configuration can enable other messages, including convention findings
on these same files. Pylint uses
[bit-encoded exit codes](https://pylint.readthedocs.io/en/stable/user_guide/usage/run.html#exit-codes),
so inspect the diagnostics before classifying a nonzero result.

For your project, run a chosen module or package in an environment with its
dependencies and reviewed Pylint configuration. Inspect import resolution before
suppressing diagnostics, and keep plugin choices explicit. For complementary
lint and type checks with retained reports, follow
[Check Python linting and types together](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/python-checks/).

## Interpret the result

Review individual diagnostic codes and locations. A summary score is not a measure of security or an accuracy benchmark. Missing dependencies, generated attributes, ignored messages, and plugin behavior can change what Pylint sees. Run application tests after code changes.

# Pyright

## Where it fits

Pyright provides another Python type-checking workflow alongside [mypy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/mypy/). It complements [Ruff](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/ruff/) linting; these tools answer different questions.

## First try

**Illustrative example; not executed here.** This path uses Pyright 1.1.407's
npm CLI with Node.js 24 and a Python 3.13 target. In a new example directory,
install the pinned checker locally:

```sh
npm install --save-dev pyright@1.1.407
```

Save `sample.py`:

```python
def double(value: int) -> int:
    return value * 2

double("two")
```

Save `pyrightconfig.json` beside it:

```json
{
  "include": ["sample.py"],
  "pythonVersion": "3.13",
  "typeCheckingMode": "strict"
}
```

Check the file without executing it:

```sh
npx --no-install pyright --project pyrightconfig.json
```

Expect an argument-type diagnostic at `double("two")`: a string does not fit
the integer parameter. Replace it with `double(2)` and repeat the command.
That diagnostic should disappear. Preserve the configuration and installed
checker version; diagnostic wording can change between releases.

The [pinned package metadata](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/1.1.407/packages/pyright/package.json)
and [CLI reference](https://github.com/microsoft/pyright/blob/main/docs/command-line.md)
describe installation requirements and invocation. This minimal file has no
third-party imports.

## Start with the project environment

Point Pyright at a small package. Configure the intended Python interpreter, target version and platform, dependencies, stubs, and import paths before interpreting missing-import or unknown-type messages. Choose a diagnostic mode deliberately and review its defaults.

## Interpret the result

Check both the analyzed-file scope and the diagnostic configuration. A clean result cannot establish runtime behavior or validate arbitrary external data. Keep the configuration and checker version with comparison results.

[Compare Pyright and mypy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Fpyright%2Ctools%2Fmypy).
Use the [comparison guidance](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/mypy/#compare-python-type-checkers) to align the
two checks' scope and investigate disagreements.

documents.markdown:
# RESTler

## What it does

RESTler uses relationships between API operations to generate request sequences. For example, a resource identifier returned by a creation request can become an input to a later request. This helps reach behavior that isolated requests would miss.

Its compiler prepares the grammar; the testing and fuzzing stages send requests to the running service. Compiling an API definition alone is not a dynamic test result.

## First try

Use the [disposable HTTP API](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/api-testing/) for a supplied service,
OpenAPI schema, reset procedure, and known failing/corrected request. It includes
create/read/delete resource dependencies and separate instructions for this tool.

The RESTler 9.3.1 procedure is illustrative. The fixture and its deterministic
replay were tested, but RESTler compilation and fuzzing were not executed.
Verify request coverage and inferred dependencies before expanding a run.

## Limits

Inferred dependencies and example values may need corrections or annotations. A server error can have several causes, and multiple failing sequences can expose the same defect.

Compare [Schemathesis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/schemathesis/) for API-schema-driven property checks and [boofuzz](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/boofuzz/) for a custom protocol harness.
