documents.title: RTAMT
documents.description: Evaluate signal traces against temporal requirements using online or offline monitors.
documents.markdown:
# RTAMT ## Where it fits Use RTAMT when you already have signals to evaluate, or can stream observations from a running system. Pairing a monitor with a simulator and a search algorithm can support falsification; the monitor alone does not perform that search. ## First try **Executed on 2026-11-06:** Windows, Python 3.12.16, RTAMT 0.4.10, and antlr4-python3-runtime 4.7, using the pure-Python backend. Both the violating and corrected traces reproduced. Python 3.13 or newer is outside this release's supported range. Use the [pinned example and setup steps](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/rtamt) or the [RTAMT installation guide](https://github.com/nickovic/rtamt#installation). This smaller example evaluates the violating trace; save it as `temperature.py` and run `python temperature.py` in that environment. The requirement says that temperature must stay at or below 80 for the next two time units: ```python import rtamt spec = rtamt.StlDenseTimeSpecification() spec.declare_var("temperature", "float") spec.spec = "always[0:2](temperature <= 80)" spec.parse() trace = [[0, 70], [1, 75], [2, 85], [3, 85]] robustness = spec.evaluate(["temperature", trace]) print(robustness[0]) ``` The observed result was `[0, -5.0]`: at time zero, the two-unit interval includes a temperature of 85, five above the limit. Replacing both 85 values with 79 produced `[0, 1.0]`, a positive margin for the corrected trace. The [execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/audits/remaining-work/executions/rtamt.json) retains the versions, script digest, and both outputs. A parser or import failure is a setup failure, not a temporal evaluation.
Earlier example evidence The local check was first reported on 2026-09-21. The 2026-09-22 audit did not rerun it or locate a saved execution record. On 2026-10-29, the saved RTAMT 0.4.10 and antlr4-python3-runtime 4.7 packages failed before evaluation on Windows/Python 3.13.15 because the parser imported `typing.io`. The 2026-11-06 run uses a fresh Python 3.12.16 environment and preserves new execution evidence; it does not alter those historical audit results.
## Interpret timing carefully Choose signal semantics, units, sampling, and the available observation horizon deliberately. An online monitor may need later observations to decide a requirement about the future. The sign and magnitude of robustness describe the formula's evaluation on this trace. Boundary cases at zero need the exact predicate semantics. A missing violation in the observed data does not rule out one in another execution. See [temporal monitoring and falsification](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/temporal-monitoring-and-falsification/) for the complete workflow.

documents.description: Find Python lint violations, common mistakes, and selected security patterns with configurable built-in rules.
documents.markdown: # Ruff ## First try **Illustrative example; not executed in this review.** [Install Ruff](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/installation/), then save this as `sample.py`: ```python import math print("Ready") ``` Run this in the directory containing the file. It checks for unused imports without changing the file or loading project configuration: ```sh ruff check --isolated --select F401 sample.py ``` Representative diagnostic excerpt, not captured output (formatting varies by version): ```text sample.py:1:8: F401 `math` imported but unused ``` The location identifies the import; `F401` identifies the unused-import rule. Remove that line and repeat the check. A clean result means this selected rule found no violation in this file. ## Use it on your project Follow the [Ruff tutorial](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/tutorial/) to configure rule selection, file exclusions, and the target Python version. Run `ruff check` for linting; `ruff format` only formats code. Start without automatic fixes so you can inspect the diagnostics. ## Fixes and limitations Ruff distinguishes safe and unsafe fixes. Review proposed changes and run your tests after applying them. Record the tool version, configuration, and preview setting for repeatable results. ## Alternatives and complements Follow the [Ruff and mypy recipe](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/python-checks/) to check one project with separate lint and type reports. Pair Ruff with [mypy](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/mypy/) or [Pyright](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/pyright/) when you also need type checking. Consider [Bandit](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/bandit/) for a dedicated Python security-rule workflow. [Pylint](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/pylint/) uses inference and supports plugins; Ruff provides built-in rule families. Their rules overlap but are not interchangeable. Before switching, compare the diagnostics and plugin requirements of your project. The [official comparison](https://docs.astral.sh/ruff/faq/#how-does-ruffs-linter-compare-to-pylint) explains these differences. Use the [finding review workflow](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/reviewing-findings/) to investigate a diagnostic and verify a correction.

documents.markdown:
# S-TaLiRo

## What it does

S-TaLiRo searches for simulation inputs or initial conditions that violate a temporal requirement. A robustness score guides optimization toward a counterexample. Published workflows use MATLAB and Simulink models of cyber-physical and hybrid systems.

The tool papers discuss Metric Temporal Logic (MTL); the ARCH-COMP report also describes STL requirements. Check the syntax and monitoring semantics of the specific release you obtain.

## When it is useful

This entry provides context for reading falsification research or reproducing experiments that use MATLAB S-TaLiRo. [PSY-TaLiRo](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/psy-taliro/) is a separate Python implementation of the broader approach.

## Availability and setup

The historical project link redirected to a Google sign-in page during this review. A current downloadable release and its installation instructions could not be verified. The Free and Open source labels describe the historical toolbox, not a newly inspected distribution. The ARCH-COMP report names the GPL but does not specify its version; the superscript 3 after GPL is a project-link footnote, not a license version.

Before reproducing an experiment, match its toolbox version, model, MATLAB dependencies, and search configuration.

## Interpreting results

A violating trace is evidence against the requirement for that model and configuration. Finding no violation within a finite budget does not establish universal correctness. See [model and temporal falsification](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/model-falsification/).

# Schemathesis

## What it does

Schemathesis derives test cases from an API definition and checks the responses from the running service. It can vary inputs, reduce failing examples, and exercise related operations through stateful testing.

Useful findings include responses that contradict the declared schema and server errors caused by generated inputs. These checks complement a security scanner such as [ZAP](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/zap/); they do not imply identical security-rule coverage.

## First try

Use the [disposable HTTP API](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/api-testing/) for a supplied service,
OpenAPI schema, reset procedure, and known failing/corrected request. It includes
create/read/delete resource dependencies and separate instructions for this tool.

The guide uses a checked Python 3.13 environment and retains separate historical
Python 3.12.16 and new Python 3.13.15 execution records for Schemathesis 4.33.1.
Its [adaptation section](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/api-testing/#adapt-to-your-api) shows a bounded
CLI command for your schema, test URL, and selected operation, plus an explicit
invalid-input variant.

## Limits

Undocumented operations, incorrect schemas, inaccessible states, and missing authorization context limit testing. A schema cannot express every business requirement; additional checks may be needed.

Compare [RESTler](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/restler/) for producer-consumer request sequences and [Hypothesis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/hypothesis/) for properties over callable code.

documents.markdown:
# Semgrep CE

## What it does

Semgrep CE matches source-code structures using rules that resemble the code being checked. Rules can express security checks or project-specific conventions, including supported local taint-analysis checks.

## When it is useful

Use it when you want to turn a recognizable coding mistake into a repeatable check. A small custom rule can be easier to maintain than a manual search performed during every review.

## What to keep in mind

CE and [Semgrep Code](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/semgrep-code/) have different analysis capabilities. CE's documented data flow analysis is limited to a single function. Cross-file analysis and Pro rules are platform capabilities available even on its limited free plan; they are not features of standalone CE. Rule quality and language support influence what a scan finds.

## Getting started

Start with a small, relevant rule set, inspect the findings, and tune the rules against representative examples. Check rule licenses separately from the engine license.

### One Python call-pattern rule

**Documentation-reviewed on November 6, 2026.** The builder's first CE workflow uses Semgrep 1.184.0, Python 3.12, and a Linux host. It selects the original MIT-licensed rule in [`examples/semgrep-ce-check`](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/semgrep-ce-check), not a Registry or Pro rule set. The directory contains the rule, license, faulty/corrected inputs, and an example the rule intentionally does not cover.

**Fixture executed on Windows with Python 3.13.15.** The OSS engine found the faulty call and reported no findings for the correction or deliberately uncovered case, with no scan errors. The [execution record](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/blob/main/examples/semgrep-ce-check/evidence.md) retains versions, input hashes, and the restricted-shell startup failure. The Linux route has not been executed here.

The rule ID is `toolwiki.python.subprocess-shell-true`. It matches `subprocess.run` and `subprocess.Popen` calls with literal `shell=True`; constant propagation is disabled. The rule reports a call to review, not a demonstrated injection path. It does not trace untrusted input or calls through wrappers.

Install `semgrep==1.184.0` in an isolated Python environment using the [host prerequisites](https://docs.semgrep.dev/prerequisites), then run from the fixture directory:

```sh
semgrep scan --oss-only --config rule.yml --no-rewrite-rule-ids --metrics off --disable-version-check --error --json bad.py
semgrep scan --oss-only --config rule.yml --no-rewrite-rule-ids --metrics off --disable-version-check --error --json good.py
```

The intended first result identifies the literal shell-enabled call in `bad.py`. The correction passes an argument list to the Python executable with `shell=False`; the input text is a process argument. It should no longer match this rule. Neither command runs the target functions. Read any scan errors and skipped-file summary before interpreting the result.

`--error` makes a completed finding produce status `1`. A parse or configuration error is a different outcome. Keep the JSON report, CLI version, and exact rule with the [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). The fixture's evidence record identifies the reviewed rule digest and any actual execution separately.

Other rules, Python call shapes, languages, and framework models remain outside this matching workflow. [Execution and data boundaries](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/execution-and-data/#semgrep-ce-with-local-rules) explains local rules, metrics, and platform reporting.

## Related research

**Related product family:** The [OCPP study](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf) used Semgrep alongside SonarQube and language-specific analyzers. It does not supply enough edition detail to attribute its results specifically to today's CE engine or Semgrep Code.

Read [comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/) for lessons about rule scope, execution failures, and zero-finding runs. Use the current CE scope above when selecting a configuration.

documents.description: Find quoting mistakes, portability problems, and other bugs in shell scripts without executing them.
documents.markdown:
# ShellCheck

## Where it fits

Use ShellCheck on shell scripts in local projects, build steps, or CI jobs. It reports diagnostic codes with explanations, making it useful for reviewing a script without executing its commands.

Choose the intended dialect. A script meant for POSIX `sh` can have portability problems even when it happens to run under Bash on your machine.

For PowerShell scripts and modules, use [PSScriptAnalyzer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/psscriptanalyzer/). PowerShell is a separate source language and is outside ShellCheck's dialects.

## Worked example: an unquoted expansion

**Illustrative example, not run here.** Save this as `sample.sh`:

```sh
#!/bin/sh
file_name='quarterly report.txt'
printf '%s\n' $file_name
```

Analyze the file with ShellCheck installed:

```sh
shellcheck sample.sh
```

The intended SC2086 warning concerns word splitting and filename expansion. For this example, change the last argument to `"$file_name"` and run the check again. Quoting preserves the value as one argument; it is not merely a formatting preference.

## Limits and configuration

Source-file resolution and dynamic code can affect what is visible to the analyzer. Set source paths and external-source options deliberately, and explain diagnostic suppressions. Use the matching diagnostic's documentation before accepting a suggested change.

ShellCheck does not execute the script to verify filesystem state, external command results, or operational effects. Keep runtime tests for those behaviors, and record the tool version and shell selection with review results.

documents.markdown:
# SonarQube Server

## What it does

SonarQube Server brings static-analysis findings into a shared view of code quality and security. Analysis rules identify issues, and quality gates evaluate results against configured conditions.

## When it is useful

Use it when you want recurring analysis and a consistent review process across projects. It can help keep security findings alongside reliability and maintainability concerns.

## Editions matter

The SonarQube name covers multiple products. This entry focuses on commercial Server editions. [Community Build](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/sonarqube-community/) has its own catalog entry so free-edition searches use its supported languages. Cloud and IDE products also have their own scope.

Check language availability and specific security features for the edition you plan to use. Do not assume that a language being supported means all analysis types are available for it.

## What to keep in mind

A passing quality gate means the configured conditions passed. It is not a guarantee that the code has no vulnerabilities. For comparisons with other tools, record the edition, analyzer versions, rule profile, and exclusions.

## Getting started

Choose the relevant product and edition, then analyze a small representative project. Review the rule profile and findings before defining quality gates for a larger workflow.

## Related research

- **Used in a case study:** [SAST in CI/CD](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/sast-workflow/) explains the SonarQube-to-GitLab integration and developer feedback. [CI/CD paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.00676).
- **Used in an empirical comparison:** [Comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/) explains why the OCPP study's report counts cannot rank tools by accuracy. [OCPP paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf).
- **Discussed in a proposed approach:** [Software quality models](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/software-quality/) connects SonarQube output to quality modeling for EV charging software. [EV charging paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/Sheppard_CSR_2025.pdf).

These papers name SonarQube; their historical setups do not establish the capabilities or performance of every current Server edition or Community Build.

documents.title: SpotBugs
documents.description: Find Java bug patterns in compiled class files, with optional security checks from Find Security Bugs.
documents.markdown: # SpotBugs ## What it examines SpotBugs reads compiled Java artifacts and looks for known defect patterns. A JAR is a container for bytecode and resources; selecting Binaries in the catalog does not mean SpotBugs accepts an arbitrary ELF or Windows executable. Use it for Java defect checks without running the application. [JBMC](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/jbmc/) offers a different workflow: checking modeled behavior against safety properties and assertions. ## First try **Illustrative example, not run here.** Use a JDK 11 environment and the [SpotBugs command-line distribution](https://spotbugs.readthedocs.io/en/stable/running.html) for the selected 4.10.x release. Confirm that release accepts your generated bytecode. Save `NullLength.java`: ```java public class NullLength { public static int length() { String value = null; return value.length(); } } ``` Compile and inspect the class: ```sh javac -g NullLength.java spotbugs -textui -xml:withMessages -output spotbugs.xml NullLength.class ``` Open `spotbugs.xml` and look for the `NP_ALWAYS_NULL` bug pattern attributed to `NullLength.length`. The report connects a pattern to a class, method, and source line when debug information is available; see the [null-dereference pattern reference](https://spotbugs.readthedocs.io/en/stable/bugDescriptions.html#np-null-pointer-dereference-np-always-null). This is an expected finding, not captured output. Change `String value = null;` to `String value = "ready";`, recompile, and rerun the same command. The expected null-dereference finding should disappear. The application is not executed. For a real project, analyze its compiled artifacts with dependencies available and keep missing-class warnings separate from a completed check. ## Optional security plugin Find Security Bugs extends SpotBugs with security detectors and framework knowledge. Record the plugin version and enabled checks when comparing it with a SAST tool. A core-only run and a plugin-enabled run are different configurations. ## Limits and comparisons Review findings in context and record exclusions. Missing dependencies, unsupported bytecode, or an unmatched pattern can leave defects undiscovered. See [Java source and bytecode analysis](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/java-analysis/) for a comparison with CodeQL and JBMC. ## Related research **Used in a study:** The [OCPP paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf) used SpotBugs for the Java implementation. Its discussion contrasts targeted bug-pattern findings with the broader quality findings reported by SonarQube. It does not establish that one tool is more accurate. Read [comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/). The paper's mention of SpotBugs does not establish use of the optional Find Security Bugs plugin; keep plugin-enabled coverage separate.

documents.description: Detect Go bugs, suspicious API use, simplification opportunities, and performance-related code issues.
documents.markdown:
# Staticcheck

## What it does

Staticcheck analyzes Go packages to flag likely bugs and questionable code. Its check families include correctness checks, simplifications, style checks, and unused-code detection. Examples include ineffective operations, incorrect use of standard-library APIs, and code that can be simplified.

Performance-related diagnostics point to code patterns; they are not runtime profiling or measurements of a program's actual latency.

## Inputs and workflow

Provide a buildable Go project with dependencies available to the Go toolchain. The command accepts package patterns like the Go tools do. Configure the target Go version and relevant build tags, and choose the package set you intend to check.

Findings carry a check identifier, source location, and explanation. The command can run locally, in CI, or through editor integrations. Use the individual check documentation to understand the condition behind a diagnostic.

## Scope and limitations

Code excluded by a platform setting or build tag needs a corresponding analysis configuration if you want it checked. A run for one build configuration does not cover every possible build.

Some checks concern style or simplification; others indicate correctness problems. Their identifiers and descriptions help distinguish those cases. Use narrow suppressions when a finding is inapplicable, and preserve the explanation for future reviewers.

## A useful first evaluation

Run Staticcheck alongside the Go toolchain's existing checks on a representative package set. Resolve package-loading or build errors, review the most relevant findings, and choose which checks should fail CI. Record the analyzer version, Go version, build tags, and package selection so future results are comparable.

documents.title: StrykerJS
documents.description: Change selected JavaScript source expressions temporarily and check whether an existing test suite notices.
documents.markdown:
# StrykerJS

## First try

Use the [JavaScript boundary-test fixture](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/test-evidence/#check-test-sensitivity).
It starts with passing tests and mutates one small function in a temporary copy.
The source under test stays unchanged; only the test assertions differ between
the two runs.

**Executed with StrykerJS 9.0.1, Jest 29.7.0, and Node.js 24.22.1 on Windows.**
Changing `total >= 100` to `total > 100` survived tests of 50 and 150. Adding an
assertion that 100 qualifies killed that mutation. The example's six generated
mutants were then killed. That result applies to this function, mutation set,
and test suite.

## Interpret a survivor

Read the changed expression and the tests that ran. Find an input where the
mutant changes required behavior, then add an assertion for that behavior. If
there is no observable difference, the mutation may be equivalent. Document
that reasoning before excluding it; do not chase 100% by adding meaningless
checks.

Read the [state and score guide](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/test-evidence/#read-mutation-outcomes)
before treating a score as evidence. A test failure that kills a mutant differs
from a test-runner error. A timeout counts as detected in Stryker's score, but
its cause still needs review.

Source mutation changes the program. [Input mutation in fuzzing](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/concepts/verification-and-generated-tests/)
changes values supplied to it. The two techniques are complementary, not interchangeable.

This profile is catalog-only while runner-specific preparation remains outside
the system builder's reviewed workflow set.

documents.title: Trivy
documents.description: Find known package vulnerabilities and infrastructure misconfigurations in container images, dependency inventories, and configuration files.
documents.markdown:
# Trivy

## Choose the input and scanner

Trivy inspects artifacts without executing the target application. A repository scan can inspect dependency files and infrastructure definitions; it does not imply general source-code analysis.

Image and repository targets can expose different package metadata. An SBOM is also an input option, but results depend on its format and completeness. Compare [OSV-Scanner](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/osv-scanner/) for another dependency-vulnerability workflow.

## Example workflows

**Illustrative commands, not run here.** With Trivy installed and its data available, enter a project containing supported dependency files:

```sh
trivy fs --scanners vuln .
```

To inspect infrastructure configuration in the current directory instead:

```sh
trivy config .
```

The first command selects vulnerability matching. The second checks supported configuration files. Misconfiguration scanning is not enabled by default in the `image`, `fs`, and `repo` commands; select it explicitly when needed.

## Inspect a container image

**Illustrative command; not executed here.** Replace `IMAGE_REFERENCE` with the
image you intend to inspect, preferably an immutable registry digest such as
`REGISTRY/PROJECT/IMAGE@sha256:DIGEST`. Those uppercase terms are placeholders.
Prepare registry access and Trivy's vulnerability data using the
[image-target guide](https://trivy.dev/docs/latest/guide/target/container_image/).
An image in a local container engine needs access to that engine; a private
registry may require authentication.

```sh
trivy image --scanners vuln IMAGE_REFERENCE
```

For an existing image archive, use the guide's `--input` route instead of a
registry reference. Record the image identity and database state. Inspect the
package, installed version, advisory, and fixed version in each finding. Trivy
does not run the image, and a package match does not establish exploitability.

## Interpret findings

For related workflows, compare [Grype](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/grype/) for package vulnerabilities, [Checkov](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/checkov/) for infrastructure policies, and [Hadolint](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/hadolint/) for Dockerfile linting. Their input and finding categories differ.

For a vulnerability, inspect the identified package, installed version, advisory source, and available fix. For configuration findings, review the affected resource and rule in the context of the intended deployment.

Different inventories and data sources can produce different reports. Record the scanner version, database state, target identity, selected scanners, and exclusions before comparing runs. A package match is evidence to investigate, not proof that an attacker can reach the vulnerable code.

[Compare Trivy and OSV-Scanner](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Ftrivy%2Ctools%2Fosv-scanner) by inputs, findings, setup, and scope.

## Compare package scanners

Trivy and OSV-Scanner both match identified packages to vulnerability data.
Compare them on the same image digest or dependency snapshot, checking which
packages each actually extracted. Their supported artifacts and advisory sources
can differ, so a larger finding count alone does not establish a better scan.
Use the [OSV-Scanner artifact table](https://google.github.io/osv-scanner/supported-languages-and-lockfiles/)
and [Trivy coverage table](https://trivy.dev/docs/latest/guide/coverage/language/)
for the input in hand.

Trivy's separate configuration checks answer a different question about
infrastructure definitions. This comparison does not attribute those checks to
OSV-Scanner or turn either tool into a general source-code analyzer.

Check the [execution and data boundaries](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/execution-and-data/) for database retrieval, telemetry, and offline preparation.

documents.markdown:
# TypeScript compiler (tsc)

## First try

**Executed on Windows with TypeScript 6.0.3 and Node.js 24.22.1.** The faulty fixture produced `TS2345`; the corrected fixture completed without diagnostics. Neither emitted JavaScript or ran the target.

Use the repository's [`examples/typescript-check`](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/typescript-check) directory. Its shared configuration enables `strict` and `noEmit`; separate project files select the faulty and corrected source. Install the pinned compiler from that directory:

```sh
npm install
npm run check:bad
```

The faulty file passes a number to a string parameter:

```ts
function greet(name: string): string {
  return name.toUpperCase();
}

greet(42);
```

The expected diagnostic is `TS2345` at the call: a number cannot be assigned to the string parameter. The fixed version calls `greet("Ada")`. Check it with the same options:

```sh
npm run check:good
```

The scripts use `tsc --project tsconfig.bad.json` or `tsconfig.good.json`. Preserve that project invocation: passing source filenames directly is a different invocation and does not apply the project's configuration in the same way. Use `tsc --showConfig --project tsconfig.good.json` to inspect the effective options.

## JavaScript needs explicit checking

For JavaScript, include the intended `.js` files and enable both `allowJs` and `checkJs`, or use the documented per-file opt-in. JSDoc and declaration files affect the available type information. This qualification is separate from the TypeScript matching workflow; a JavaScript language tag alone does not establish that checking is enabled.

## Use it with ESLint

[ESLint](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/eslint/) applies selected coding rules. Its TypeScript integration can use type information, but it does not replace the compiler's type-checking pass. Run each for its own diagnostics and retain separate reports. Use runtime tests and input validation for behavior and data that static types cannot establish.

When adapting the fixture, choose the actual project files, module settings, library declarations, and strictness. Check exclusions and suppressions before interpreting a clean result. Keep versions and the configuration with the [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/).

documents.markdown:
# UndefinedBehaviorSanitizer (Clang)

## Where it fits

Use UBSan to make selected arithmetic and pointer mistakes visible during tests. Compare [AddressSanitizer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/address-sanitizer/) for other memory errors and [ThreadSanitizer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/thread-sanitizer/) for data races.

## Worked example: signed overflow

**Illustrative example, not run here.** Save this as `overflow.c` in a Clang environment with UBSan support:

```c
#include <limits.h>

int main(void) {
    volatile int largest = INT_MAX;
    return largest + 1;
}
```

In a Unix-style shell, build and exercise it:

```sh
clang -O0 -g -fsanitize=undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=undefined overflow.c -o overflow
./overflow
```

Expect a signed-overflow diagnostic and a failing execution. This is an intended outcome, not captured output. Replacing the addition with `largest - 1` removes this example's overflow.

## Interpret the result

The `undefined` group is not every available check; unsigned overflow, for example, requires separate selection. Compiler flags control recovery and trap behavior.

Keep the workload and build flags with each result. A clean run says nothing about paths that were not exercised. [Compare the three sanitizers](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/compare/?tools=tools%2Faddress-sanitizer%2Ctools%2Fundefined-behavior-sanitizer%2Ctools%2Fthread-sanitizer), or read the [memory-checking workflow](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/memory-error-detection/).

# Valgrind Helgrind

## Where it fits

Helgrind adds a concurrency-focused option beside [ThreadSanitizer](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/thread-sanitizer/). It is a separate Valgrind tool from [Memcheck](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/valgrind-memcheck/).

## Exercise the shared state

Run a reproducible threaded workload with Helgrind selected. Review the accesses and synchronization reported together, rather than treating the final stack frame as the entire explanation.

## Account for synchronization models

Helgrind works best with pthreads. Check its guidance before interpreting custom synchronization or adding annotations. Retain representative concurrency tests: one execution cannot cover all schedules.

documents.title: Valgrind Memcheck
documents.description: Detect invalid memory access, uninitialized-value use, and leaks while a native program runs.
documents.markdown: # Valgrind Memcheck ## What it does Memcheck observes a program's memory operations during execution. It reports problems such as invalid reads and writes, incorrect deallocation, use of uninitialized values, and memory leaks. ## When it is useful Use it to investigate memory behavior while running representative native-code tests. Debug information helps relate reports to the source. ## What to keep in mind It analyzes the execution you exercise. An untested path can still contain a defect. Instrumentation also slows execution, and platform support must be checked before planning a workflow. Memcheck is dynamic analysis, but it is not a web DAST scanner. ## First try **Illustrative example; not executed here.** This path targets [Valgrind 3.28.0](https://valgrind.org/downloads/) on amd64 Linux with a C compiler such as GCC. Install it through your distribution or the release instructions. Native Windows is outside this path. Save `memory.c`: ```c #include int main(void) { int *values = malloc(4 * sizeof(*values)); if (values == NULL) return 1; values[4] = 7; free(values); return 0; } ``` Build with debug information, then run under Memcheck: ```sh cc -g -O0 memory.c -o memory valgrind --tool=memcheck --leak-check=full ./memory ``` Expect an invalid-write report at `values[4]`: the allocation has indices 0 through 3. Inspect the stack and allocation context, not just the final error count. Change the write to `values[3]`, rebuild, and rerun with the same options. The invalid write should disappear; a failed allocation is a separate execution outcome, not a successful check of that write. The [official quick start](https://valgrind.org/docs/manual/quick-start.html) explains debug builds and report structure. For your application, retain its normal input arguments, the binary identity, and any suppressions in a [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/). Memcheck checks the paths actually run; use representative tests and review errors before adding narrow suppressions.

documents.markdown:
# VerifAI

## What the workflow does

A sampler proposes a scenario, the simulator runs it, and a monitor evaluates the resulting behavior. Feedback can guide later scenarios toward violations. This supports questions such as whether a controller stays inside its lane under varying initial conditions.

## Worked example: lane-keeping falsification

**Documentation-based walkthrough, not run here.** Install the repository version and dependencies for the official lane-keeping example. The PyPI package does not include all example files.

In two terminals, enter `src/verifai/simulators/car_simulator` within the matching repository checkout. In the first terminal, start the falsifier:

```sh
python examples/lanekeeping_LQR/lanekeeping_falsifier.py
```

After the server reports readiness, start the simulator in the second terminal:

```sh
python examples/lanekeeping_LQR/lanekeeping_simulation.py
```

Inspect sampled scenarios, their requirement scores, and the falsified-sample table. In this quantitative example, a negative score indicates a violation. Re-run the saved scenario to check reproducibility before changing the controller.

## What to preserve with a result

Record the simulator revision, scenario ranges, requirement, sampling configuration, budget, and any random seed. A successful trace says something about that modeled execution, not every scenario or the physical system.

Compare [Breach](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/breach/) and [PSY-TaLiRo](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/psy-taliro/) for other falsification workflows. [RTAMT](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/rtamt/) focuses on monitoring supplied signals; see [temporal monitoring and falsification](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/temporal-monitoring-and-falsification/).

# Verilator (HDL lint)

## First try

**Illustrative example, not executed here.** Use the
[5.054 installation guide](https://github.com/verilator/verilator/blob/v5.054/docs/guide/install.rst)
and confirm `verilator --version`. The fixture is in
[`examples/verilator`](https://github.com/zwadhams/ToolWiki/tree/main/examples/verilator).
Run from that directory on Linux. It has one module, no included files, and no
preprocessor definitions.

The faulty assignment narrows an eight-bit input into a four-bit output without
stating which bits to retain. Check it with the source list, language standard,
top module, and warning flag explicit:

```sh
verilator --lint-only --language 1800-2017 --top-module width_demo -Wwarn-WIDTHTRUNC bad/width_demo.sv
```

Expect `WIDTHTRUNC` at the assignment. Inspect the reported widths and location;
the output shown by your run is the evidence, not this expectation. Warnings are
fatal by default, so a warning can cause a nonzero exit. An unsupported-language
error or missing source is an incomplete check.

The corrected fixture explicitly selects `word[3:0]`, assuming the low four bits
are intended. Run the same options against it:

```sh
verilator --lint-only --language 1800-2017 --top-module width_demo -Wwarn-WIDTHTRUNC good/width_demo.sv
```

The truncation warning should disappear. This establishes the intended source
change for that check; it does not test the design's behavior. For a real
project, record all source files, `-I` include paths, `-D` definitions, warning
changes, and the top module in a [run record](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/guides/run-record/).

## Keep lint separate from simulation

This profile uses `--lint-only`, which does not generate a simulation model.
Other Verilator modes can generate C++ or SystemC, but those output languages
are not input-language tags for this workflow. Simulation results and hardware
proof obligations need their own tools, harnesses, and evidence.

documents.description: Apply selected Scala compiler checks to constructs that can weaken type safety or hide mistakes.
documents.markdown:
# WartRemover

## What it does

WartRemover checks Scala code during compilation. Each wart describes a construct to flag, such as calling `get` on an `Option`, where an empty value would throw. You decide which restrictions suit the project.

## Example

**Illustrative configuration, not run here.** In a compatible sbt project, add to `project/plugins.sbt`:

```scala
addSbtPlugin("org.wartremover" % "sbt-wartremover" % "3.6.2")
```

Enable one warning in `build.sbt`:

```scala
wartremoverWarnings += Wart.OptionPartial
```

Then run `sbt compile` on code containing an `Option.get` call. The intended warning identifies that partial operation. Refactoring to explicitly handle empty and nonempty cases addresses the rule's concern.

## Limits

Installing the plugin alone does not establish that any warts ran: the documented warning and error rule lists are empty by default. Record the selected warts and suppressions with the results.

A warning can enforce a team convention even when the particular call is safe under an assumption. Review the context instead of treating every wart as a vulnerability.

## Related research

We used WartRemover for the Scala implementation in our [OCPP study](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/CSR_2026_Wadhams.pdf). The reported tool name alone does not establish which checks were enabled; see [Comparing SAST tools](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/comparing-tools/).

documents.title: YARA-X
documents.description: Scan file contents using rules that combine text, byte patterns, and conditions.
documents.markdown:
# YARA-X

## What it does

YARA-X evaluates rules over files. A rule can combine recognizable strings, hexadecimal patterns, regular expressions, and conditions. This is useful for grouping related artifacts or checking for a specific marker.

The original YARA project is in maintenance mode, with new development focused on YARA-X. Existing rules should still be checked against the documented compatibility differences.

## Example

**Illustrative example, not run here.** Save this harmless marker rule as `marker.yar`:

```text
rule WikiMarker {
    strings:
        $marker = "TOOLWIKI_SAMPLE"
    condition:
        $marker
}
```

Create `sample.bin` containing the ASCII text `TOOLWIKI_SAMPLE`, then run:

```sh
yr scan marker.yar sample.bin
```

The intended result is a `WikiMarker` match. Removing the marker should remove that match. This establishes a byte-pattern condition, not a vulnerability.

## Limits

Rules can match benign files or miss changed and encoded content. Preserve the rule revision with the artifact. Compare [capa](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/capa/) for capability rules over extracted features and [FLOSS](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/tools/floss/) for recovering obscured strings.

## Related research

Our [malware sophistication paper](https://www.cs.montana.edu/izurieta/pubs/iETC_Porcella_2026.pdf) discusses the original YARA, not YARA-X. We did not evaluate YARA-X. See [Malware sophistication](https://zwadhams.github.io/ToolWiki/research/binary-analysis/).

documents.title: ZAP
documents.description: Inspect web traffic and test running web applications with passive and active security checks.
documents.markdown:
# ZAP

## What it does

ZAP proxies and inspects web traffic. Passive checks examine messages, while active scanning sends test requests to investigate potential vulnerabilities. Discovery and authentication determine which parts of an application it reaches.

## When it is useful

Use it to investigate the behavior of a running web application or include security checks in a test workflow. Logged-in functionality requires suitable authentication setup.

## What to keep in mind

Crawling is discovery, not proof of security coverage. Passive checks and active tests reveal different kinds of evidence. An active scan can change application state, so use an authorized test environment.

## Getting started

Start by observing a small test application's traffic. Review the difference between passive and active scanning, then configure the target scope and any login flow before expanding the test.
